Terming the protest by the Congress over the cancellation of the land allotment as "drama", Mayawati said it was enacted by the Congress only to draw political mileage ahead of the Lok Sabha polls.

The fact, however, is that the government had tied itself in knots while explaining its action.

* It claimed to have taken back the land on the basis of a report from the District Magistrate which said that there was resentment among villagers and this might lead to self-immolations and a "Singur-like" situation. However, it soon became clear that there was no resentment against the project; in fact, locals, including her own partymen, wanted the project to come up and the resentment was against the government's action.

* Soon, the government stopped talking of the anger of the farmers. Instead, it tried to defend its action by arguing that the allotment suffered from serious procedural flaws such as the absence of a cabinet approval.

* However, one of Mayawati's principal secretaries, Vijay Shanker Pandey, in his capacity as Divisional Commissioner of Lucknow, had been dealing with the matter all along. However, while Principal Secretary (Revenue) Balwinder Kumar and another Principal Secretary to Chief Minister V N Garg were removed after the "fiasco", Pandey was elevated and posted as additional cabinet secretary.

* The biggest problem, however, was defending the cancellation in the high court. The allotment was made after the Railways had completed all formalities and paid the cost of land. The entries in the revenue records were in Railway's favour and it had already spent a lot of money on developing the land. On a petition moved by the Union Government and the Railways, the Lucknow bench of the Allahabad High Court ordered that the Railways' possession of the land will not be disturbed, restrained the UP government from allotting the land to anyone else, and fixed the next hearing for October 22.

State Congress president Rita Bahuguna Joshi described the decision as the victory of the struggle of the people of Rae Bareli and Amethi.

Heading: DC Model School wins inter-school declamation contest - Indian Express
Content:
The senior residents at the PGI called off their strike after observing a one-day mass casual leave following a controversy in which the Urology department's assistant professor allegedly slapped and shouted at a senior resident.

A single day of the absence of as many as 800 resident doctors severely paralysed the normal OPD functioning at the institute. All the scheduled surgeries were cancelled as most of the rooms of the senior residents remained locked in the OPD block. The senior faculty too attended far lesser number of patients than the usual days. It was only the emergency and the ICU services were not affected during the day.

After the late evening meeting of the Association of Resident Doctors (ARD), Dr Prabhu Shanker, president of the association, said, "In the larger interest of patients, we have decided to abort the strike and resume work from Sunday. The director has promised us that the matter will be taken up at the level of the health minister."

Despite a written apology by the consultant, the residents want the matter to be taken to the Health Minister for a disciplinary action. They are also seeking a public apology from him.

The incident occurred when Dr Sanand Kumar, senior resident, Urology, was allegedly assaulted and abused by Dr Santhosh Kumar, assistant professor of the same department, in front of the hospital staff. The tiff began after Dr Santhosh found his patient was listed number two by the resident doctor in the operation theatre list for the day even as he had wanted him to be on the number one slot. Reportedly, the professor lost his cool and the abused the senior resident for making the change without telling him.

The three-member committee comprising Dean Prof V Sakhuja, Sub Dean Prof Amod Gupta and Prof Savita Malhotra of the Department of Psychiatry was appointed to inquire into the matter. Dr Santhosh was found guilty of using unparliamentary language in the heat of the moment and was asked to proceed on leave.

"We have examined the case closely. The consultant has admitted that he misbehaved in a fit of rage and has now tendered his unconditional apology in the writing. He even went to the Dr Sanand Kumar's hostel to aplogise but the resident doctor was not there," said Prof Amod Gupta.

Doctor speak: Dr Santhosh Kumar said: "I reacted in the heat of the moment. My conduct was not for my individual gain but out of my concern for my patient. Unfortunately, it is the chief senior resident who makes the list of the operation theatre cases without even consulting the senior faculty. Even in the past, such lack of communication and lack of system has led to tussle and arguments between the senior residents and the consultants. I had earlier also informed the head of the department about the problem, but to no avail. That's the reason I felt even more suffocated and acted in rage. In any case, I have explained everything to the hospital administration and tendered my unconditional apologies to the director in the writing. I will follow what the hospital administration decides."

A K Gupta, Deputy Director Administration: "We have sent letters to the senior residents for not reporting on duty and the matter is being viewed sternly. Not performing your duty and resorting to mass casual leave is not the right way to protest. The power of dismissing or suspending the faculty member, as demanded by the residents, is not in the purview of the PGI authorities. It is the prerogative of the governing body."

Heading: Why blood relations are becoming bloody? - Indian Express
Content:

Heading: ‘Govt should promote cadaver donation in India’ - Indian Express
Content:
On September 30, three murders were reported from different areas of the city. During investigations, the police found that two of these crimes were committed by close relatives of the deceased. While in one case a man was killed by his son, the other murder was committed by the brother of the deceased.

Atma Singh, who worked as a watchman, was allegedly killed by his son Gurdeep Singh. A youth, Harinder Singh, according to the police, was murdered by his brother Narinder Singh. Both the accused have been arrested.

These two cases are not the isolated example of murders committed by relatives. In a short span of one month, at least eight such incidents have come to light from in and around the city.

On October 1, the police claimed to have solved the case of murder of one Rishipal, with the arrest of his son Sunny Mehra and deceased's brother-in-law Mukesh Kumar along with three others. Rishipal was found murdered on February 6 this year.

Earlier, one Randhir Singh was shot dead by his nephew near Raikot on September 28. Two days before that, one Rajesh Kumar had strangulated his wife Rinku to death in Baba Namdev Nagar and later hid the body in a trunk. On September 25, in a gruesome incident, ex-armyman Lakhvir Singh allegedly butchered to death his father and brother at Kotla Bharri village near Khanna. Lakhvir also severely injured his mother, another brother, brother's wife, and his six-year-old nephew.

It's not only men who have been accused of killing their family members and relatives. The Ludhiana rural (Jagraon) police have arrested one Jatinderpal Kaur for hatching conspiracy to kill her NRI husband Basant Singh, whose body was found on September 23.

According to the police, Jatinderpal, along with her nephew Baljinder Singh, with whom she is alleged to have illicit relations, had planned to kill her husband. The police said she had hatched the conspiracy when she was in Finland with her husband. The husband, who returned home on September 15, was kidnapped from outside a dhaba at Jagraon on September 19 and his body was found on September 23. The police also arrested Baljinder with three others in connection with the murder.

While these cases were reported within a short span, the police ruled out that the law and order situation was out of control in the district. Gurpreet Singh Toor, SP (Detective), said: "Our investigations revealed that these murders were committed out of hatred and due to fall in the family and social values. For example, in a case a man killed his father as the latter was keeping a bad eye on the wife of the former."

"These eight murders do not mean that there is something wrong with the law and order. The police can do nothing in the cases where someone is killed by a close relative," said another senior police officer.

Toor said that in such cases, the police can do little to ensure people's security and the society as a whole should come forward to inculcate moral and social values among the people.

Heading: 2008 records highest number of dengue cases in 4 years - Indian Express
Content:
The government should promote cadaver donation in India through a comprehensive education programme, Sir Peter Morris, renowned surgeon and the Director of Oxford Radcliffe Hospital of the UK has said.

He said there is a big defect in the whole system in India, but in the UK, 70 per cent of the organ donations are through cadaver donations (brain dead pool).

Sir Morris is currently in the city to attend the 19th annual conference of the Indian Society of Organ Transplantation (ISOT).

"There are certainly not willing donors here in this country and therefore cadaver donations are just not possible. In European countries like Spain, virtually all organ transplants are carried out with cadaver donations only," he said.

Incidentally, Sir Morris was also a guest speaker at the 5th Annual Conference of North Zone Association of Plastic Surgeons hosted by the Christian Medical College and Hospital.

He said: "Every year, we conduct more than 3,000 organ transplants in the UK, which has a population of 50 million, and of them 70 per cent of the organs are transplanted from cadavers. But here in India, it is just not picking up because of what I believe are certain so-called religious myths."

He added: "The cultural hurdles are not blocking cadaver donations therefore countries like Japan and some South Eastern nations are lagging behind. In India, the Hindu public should therefore dispel such myths and consider it for the benefit of the community. The families who agree to make cadaver donations can only make this 'cultural' change take place."

He further said the government should pump in resources so that people can be made aware of this. "For example, Singapore has increased cadaver donations substantially with the help of a thoroughly charted out programme," he added.

Heading: MC challans 185 residents for not following anti-dengue norms - Indian Express
Content:
With 52 fresh cases of dengue being reported in the district on Saturday, the number of this mosquito-borne disease has risen to 1,144, the highest in the state in the last four years.

Notably, between 50 and 80 fresh cases are being reported every day for the last couple of weeks.

As many as 1,115 cases have been reported in the last 30 days at an average of 40 per day. The state has registered over 1,918 cases so far, out of which 1,309 are confirmed cases of dengue.

The Dayanand Medical College and Hospital (DMCH), where most of the patients are admitted, reported 60 more cases today, while Christian Medical College and Hospital registered 32 and the SPS Apollo Hospital five fresh cases.

"We have been observing the disease since 1996 and have figured out that there is a cyclic variation in its outbreaks. It has been taking place every third year, but this time it struck in the second year after 2006. The high temperature has also been a reason," said Dr Sandeep Puri, medical superintendent, DMCH.

With no let up in the cases, both the Health department and MC officials have pinned hopes on the decrease in temperature so that the number of dengue cases comes down.

Dr Deepak Bhatia, co-ordinator of the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project in the state, said, "We are expecting the pace at which the cases are being reported to slow down in the next six-seven days."

Dr JP Mangla, district epidemiologist, said the Health department has been apprising the MC of the situation on a regular basis.

"We have repeatedly been holding meetings with MC officials and have also told them about some residents complaining about incomplete fogging operations in various areas of the city," said Mangla.

Heading: I once wanted to be a doctor, but could not, so I bow to them: CM - Indian Express
Content:
The Municipal Corporation, Ludhiana has challaned 185 residents from across the city for not complying with anti-dengue norms.

MC Commissioner G S Ghuman told Newsline that a fine of Rs 500 each has been imposed on the residents who were not following the preventive measures against dengue.

"If they will not pay the fine within seven days, Rs 500 will be added to the amount everyday," Ghuman said, adding, "Our teams are doing random checking all across the city."

He further said, "Residents need to be careful as they also have the responsibility of preventing outbreak of such diseases rather than indulging in blame game."

Sources said that not even a single violator has paid the fine till Saturday, even as the deadline for most of them will end on Monday.

The violations found in the challaned cases included standing water in flowerpots among others. However dengue larvae was not checked in any of these houses due to lack of co-ordination.

Dr Charanjit Uppal, Medical Officer Health, Municipal Corporation, said, "We have informed the health teams. It is duty of the Health department to take samples of water from all these houses."

However, experts feel that ideally, the health and MC teams should go together so as to take the samples on the spot, but nothing of this sort has been planned as of now.

Heading: CPM’s youth wing demands arrest of Partho - Indian Express
Content:
Promises to bring in laws for easier organ donation process

"I also wanted to be a doctor but after spending some time with studies in medicine, I realised it was difficult for me to be a doctor so I changed stream," said Chief Minister Prakash Singh Badal at the inaugural ceremony of 19th annual conference of Indian Society of Organ Transplantation.

He expressed his gratitude towards doctors and said: "I bow to them who are involved in the task of saving lives."

In a lighter vein, he, however, added: "Though today I think I am doing a more difficult job of being a politician. But the doctors need to be given their due in every sense."

He told delegates from various parts of the country and abroad who were present at the inaugural ceremony that the government is willing to introduce any requisite law to promote organ donation in the state.

"The state government will do whatever is required to make organ donation easier. I assure the conference that the state government will leave no stone unturned and will take all measures to promote this," he said. This is for the first time the ISOT annual conference is being held in the state.

He however, added that for this, the state government requires better infrastructure along with transportation and storage facilities for the organs. Also, computerised data of the recipients and potential donors is also required to be prepared in this regard, he said.

He said it was a noble cause to donate organs and therefore awareness was required among the people.

He, however, felt strongly about the healthcare services in the rural areas.

"DMCH is by far one of the best institutions where patients from abroad also come for treatment. But we need similar standards of healthcare in our rural areas too. I request doctors of such institutions to hold a meeting with doctors of rural areas and apprise them about their duty and high standards of healthcare which, sadly, some of them are not following."

Heading: ‘New measures must for curbing cyber crime’ - Indian Express
Content:
At a rally held in the city on Saturday, the youth wing of the CPM, Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI), demanded immediate arrest of Trinamool Congress leader and Leader of the Opposition, Partho Chatterjee. He is alleged to have threatened Police Commissioner Gautam Mohan Chakrabarti over phone during the recent Charu Market incident.

The youth wing also submitted a deputation to Chakrabarti at Lalbazar, Kolkata police headquarters.

"The Trinamool Congress is trying to bring in anarchy and lawlessness in the state. They are helping anti-socials to run amok in the city streets of which the recent Charu Market incident is a glaring example," said Tirthankar Mukherjee, Kolkata district secretary of DYFI, while addressing around 2,000 people in the rally.

"How can a politician say that if his party workers are arrested he will burn Bengal? Trinamool chief Mamata Banerjee and her party are against development," added Mukherjee.

The DYFI leader also announced that street corner meetings will be organised throughout Kolkata and suburbs on October 20—the same day Mamata Banerjee will hold her siege Lalbazar Abhiyan.

Heading: Police take away woman’s body from crematorium for postmortem - Indian Express
Content:
Commissioner of Kolkata Police Gautam Mohan Chakrabarti has said there is an urgent need for constituting an advisory group with technical experts to help the government develop cyber crime laboratories in the state.He said that besides this there is a need for promotion of training programmes by IT industries and cyber security audits by independent agencies "The crime scenario has changed. Unlike earlier days, we find educated people engaged in cyber crime," Chakrabarti said at a seminar organised by the Bengal Chamber of Commerce on cyber security on Saturday.

Experts like B J Srinath, senior director of Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said the Internet has become more popular leading to altering of crime scenes. "Automation has made cyber crime more profitable. Attack technique propagation is also easier through the Internet," he said.

Heading: Top officers transferred - Indian Express
Content:
The death of a woman on Friday sparked tension at a locality near Alochaya cinema on Beliaghata Road with the residents of the area suspecting foul play by her husband.

Locals allege that Gopa Banerjee's husband, Suhrid Banerjee-an assistant sub-inspector in river traffic police-has murdered her and was therefore trying to cremate her body quickly.

On Friday afternoon, the police reached Nimtala Ghat crematory and took away the body to Nil Ratan Sarkar (NRS) hospital to conduct a postmortem. "We detained the body after receiving a complaint from the locals. We are waiting for the postmortem report," said J N Barik, Additional O-C, Beliaghata police station.

The family of the deceased, however, refutes the allegation. Debjani, daughter of the deceased, said: "My mother had chronic asthma. On Friday she had a breathing trouble. I rushed to get the medicine but the shops were closed."

Suhrid said, "We took her to a nursing home where a doctor declared her dead. On hearing this, we took her to NRS hospital and got the same reply. There we were advised by the hospital authorities to get the death certificate from the local doctor." The family procured the death certificate from a local doctor, Dr CR Kundu, who wrote that Gopa died of "cardio respiratory failure."

Heading: Bus drivers put a brake on city’s transport - Indian Express
Content:
The West Bengal government has decided to deal with tiger poaching with an iron hand. On Friday, three top-level forest officers, including the director of Sunderban Tiger Reserve, were transferred after it was confirmed that a tiger was shot dead by poachers on October 6.

The issue came to light after a Royal Bengal Tiger was found dead in one of the ravines of Sajnekhali in the Sunderbans on October 6. Later, the CID took up the matter for investigation. The state government, meanwhile, took stern action prompted by Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee and transferred the three officers — Sunderban Tiger Reserve director Niraj Singhal, Sunderban Biosphere Reserve director Pradip Shukla and chief wildlife warden S S Bist.

"Preliminary investigation pointed towards the fact that poachers are active in Sunderbans. The tiger was shot in the head from an elevated position, twice. There were no other injury marks. We expect to make arrests soon," said Bhupinder Singh, ADJ, CID. According to the ADG, the shots were fired from a 12-bore rifle commonly used by the poachers.

State Forest Minister Ananta Roy said: "The incident has been an eye-opener for us. The officers failed to discharge their responsibilities and therefore were transferred."

"The chief minister has given us a free hand to take action. We have initiated a departmental inquiry into the incident apart from the ongoing CID probe. If other officers are found involved they will also be punished," Roy added.

Sources in the CID, meanwhile, said the probe has revealed that a wide network of poachers is active in the Sunderbans. Apart from deers and other wild animals, Royal Bengal tigers are their prime targets.

"In this case, the poachers were either sitting on a tree top or on a 'machan'. It seems that they are highly organised. Somehow, the tiger fell into the ravines after being shot and they could not get the body," said a CID officer.

Sleuths also said the network of poachers were linked to both forest officials as well as international traders engaged in trade of tiger skin and body parts. "The poachers are mostly locals and there is an elaborate network of touts who are also linked to the international market dealing with tiger parts, which are in high demand. Some of the forest officials are also directly linked with the racket," the officer added.

Heading: Briefly State - Indian Express
Content:
To protest against the filing of attempt to murder charges against some drivers involved in accident, private bus drivers in Kolkata and adjoining areas observed a strike on Saturday.

With nearly 500 bus drivers and conductors participating in the strike, passengers at the Howrah railway station and other areas of the city had a tough time.

On September 24, a private bus plying between Howrah and Irpalla (Midnapore) ran over a passenger at Daspur near Ghatal. The driver, Radhanath Manna, was charged under section 304 of the CrPC (attempt to murder). As it is a non-bailable offence, the driver is in jail since then. Earlier, drivers responsible for accidents used to be booked under section 304 A of the CrPC.

"If there are more such instances, drivers will stop driving buses or will run away from the accident site," said Shekhar Sonkar, secretary of Howrah Midnapore Private Bus Workers Association.

He demanded that drivers involved in accidents should be booked under Section 304A and the accused be released within 24 hours.

"In certain cases, accidents occur when buses try to overtake, then only harsher punishments should be meted out but not in all the cases," said CITU-backed Bengal Bus Syndicate vice-president Rabindranath Dutta, whose association did not participate in the strike but extended moral support to the striking drivers.

"Recently, the police have booked drivers under section 304 in Kolkata, Howrah, Midnapur and Malda. The solution lies in making drivers more responsible from the beginning so that they have to pay a fine for violating a signal," said Sadhan Das, president of Joint Council of Bus Syndicate.

Heading: Civic body to redevelop Andheri municipal market - Indian Express
Content:
Central team satisfied with KMC

During the visit to the health centres of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) on Saturday, a team of Union Ministry of Health & Family Welfare said the preventive measures taken in the city against dengue are satisfactory. The team comprised Pushpita Banerjee, Chief Medical Officer of ministry health and family welfare, and HG Thakur, consultant, National Vector-borne Diseases Control Programme, among others. The dengue count in the city has reached 60. Four people have died of dengue. The figures of malignant malaria cases have crossed 650 with two deaths.

IIT student held with heroin

A student of agricultural and food engineering department of IIT- Kharagpur was arrested with 100 grams of heroin on Saturday. Police, said he was arrested from within the campus.

Heading: Akbar Travels sink Indian Navy - Indian Express
Content:
Putting an end to uncertainty over which government agency would redevelop the municipal market at Andheri, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has taken up the job of constructing a mall to accommodate the displaced J P Road shopkeepers.

The decision was taken at a meeting of elected representatives chaired by Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh at Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) headquarters on Thursday. "The issue regarding the construction of the mall in place of the existing municipal market was discussed at the meeting and it was decided that BMC would redevelop it. Within a month or two, the work would start after sorting out the issues," said Metropolitan Commissioner Ratnakar Gaikwad.

According to the sources, the solution to this issue was delayed as the BMC, which owns the Andheri market, had not decided whether it would construct the mall or give the land to the MMRDA for development. "The BMC was keen to hand over the land to the MMRDA, but subsequently they decided to develop it themselves," said a senior official.

However, as many as 278 affected shopkeepers are not so thrilled after hearing the civic body's decision. They said the authorities had given many "promises" to them, but they wanted something in writing now. "We've no information about this decision. If it's decided, it's good, but we want everything on paper," said Pratap Ankolekar, working committee member of the Metro Rail Project Affected Persons Action Committee (MRPAPAC).

Accodring to him, the indecision of the authorities has been a cause of concern for the shopkeepers of JP Road. "The MMRDA is unclear about the rehabilitation policy for the displaced people at the J P Road. They are asking us to shift to Oshiwara temporarily, which is not possible, despite their promise to relocate us to Andheri market. We should be relocated within the vicinity of our existing commercial establishments and we need a permanent place in the proposed mall," Ankolekar said.

Meanwhile, Gaikwad said that construction of the 11.7 km Versova-Andheri-Ghatkopar corridor between Navrang Cinema and Andheri Station would start soon. "Construction work can start on this stretch soon. We're working to rehabilitate 17 shops," Gaikwad said.

He also said there would be no delay in the commissioning of the first metro rail due to rehabilitation issues. "We're confident that the first metro rail would be commissioned in June 2010," he said.

Heading: Red Romeo wins with plenty in saddle - Indian Express
Content:
Akbar Travels posted a comfortable 3-1 against Indian Navy in a MFL Elite Division encounter at the RCF ground in Chembur on Saturday. O Ezekal scored two goals, in the 67th and 89th minutes, and Vineeth Anthony scored the third in the 71st minute. P S Sumesh reduced the margin for Navy in the 87th minute.

In the second match, RCF's Allan Dias got the first goal in the 23rd minute after Nigel D'Souza had worked hard to create several chances for his team. After Muzzafar Ansari was red carded for elbowing Nigel D'Souza, another goal was disallowed, because Sagar Chile was ruled off-side trying to give a final touch to a goal-ward bound ball. Abbas Rizvi equalized for Bank of India in the 42nd minute when RCF custodian Nayeem Ansari let a harmless free-kick through his hands into goal. The last 25 minutes saw at least 10 chances go a begging for the RCF side, but the winner was to elude them, the game ending at 1-1.

The performance of referee Amjad Khan came in for severe criticism as he made an impact in both the day's games. He controversially red-carded Navy striker Shaji D'Silva.

Heading: Upsets galore at District table tennis - Indian Express
Content:
Nitin Mongia's team took the lead in the final race for victory and put up a splendid show to win the ISAF Nations Cup on Saturday. Both the team's strategies and courses were entirely different in order to cope up with the difficult wind conditions and the race to the finish line proved to be literally bow-to-bow. The committee vessel awarded the championship to Nitin's team.

The fight for the third place ended with Farokh Tarapore's team beating Aashim Mongia's team comprehensively. In the other semi-final Nitin Mongia's team beat Farokh Tarapore's team in a best-of-three contest.

Heading: Postcard from mumbai - Indian Express
Content:
Eco-tourism or a countryside resort, organic farms take it all in their stride

Raigad district's farmers are tense as the SEZ wave enters the district. Lands of small and large farmers here stand the risk of take-over by giant corporations, land developers and builders poised with their JCBs. In times of such seismic changes in the development paradigm of the state and the nation at large, a small group of people is trying to hold on to what may seem like a distant dream — that of nurturing and protecting the environment and teaching our children to do the same. And everyone who cares is invited to share this dream.

Van Vadi, which lies at the foot of the Sahyadris, is a haven for Bharat Mansata and for those who wish to live in harmony with nature, cultivating their own land through healthy, organic agricultural practices. Pooled in his resources with a dozen other likeminded people, Mansata acquired the lush 64-acre land 14 years ago. Van Vadi lies a kilometre from Vaara village, Neral, in Raigad district. The land has been attracting city dwellers every October since 2005 to join in for Van Utsav (a five-day festival) and Shram Utsav (for volunteering labour at their organic farms). While Mansata doesn't call this eco-tourism, what the farm offers is becoming something of a trend among vacationers. The last few years have seen powerful campaigns raising concern for the environment. "There are many who have jumped on to the eco-travel bandwagon. But with most people it's just namesake of eco-tourism, or 'Greenwash' as we call it. The concept though does have a lot of potential if done well," says Mansata.

Living in bamboo-huts without electricity, community cooking, two hours of daily farm labour or working on the construction of a house, workshops on carpentry and yoga are some of the things that encapsulate the experience at Van Vadi. There are streams in the land that are full and the vegetation lush green, fresh from the recent monsoon.

Mona Patrao, co-owner of Van Vadi runs a two-acre farm and school at Bhose village between Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, and sounds like a remnant from the flower-power days. Still fresh with ideas, she hasn't lost hope and cycled back to society like Alain Tanner's protagonist in his sublime 70s classic Jonas Who will be 25 by the Year 2000, who left mainstream society to find a better world for his daughter to grow up in, but finally lost hope and returned. "Well it was the '70s. We were all searching for a better way," says Patrao, who has been living on her farm for the last 30 years and has built an almost self-sustaining space with over a 100 different varieties of plant species, a bio-gas plant, solar parabolic heaters, grey-water recycling mechanisms. She grows carrots, lettuce, strawberries, lemon, guava, cherry tomatoes, mulberry, gooseberry, onion, garlic, ragi, sesame, potatoes and black beans according to

season. Started with her husband and educationist Peter, Redstone (Home) School, which Mona runs at the farm, attracts several school excursions from Mumbai and nearby Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar.

Patrao now works on her farm with help from local farmers and villagers who provide that vital 'indigenous wisdom' which is "crucial".

Hemant Babu, the founder member of Tamarind Tree Trust has a slightly different approach to this way of life. His is a three-acre piece of land with sanitised thatch-hut-style housing arrangements, small rice fields, a museum and a learning centre for Warli. Located in Sogwe, a small tribal village in Dahanu, about 100 km from Mumbai, Babu came here after a 15-year disillusioning career in journalism. "I like to think that what we do here is political. In involving a tribal art form, we are also trying to open up a different way of life and a debate about sustainability," he says. He eloquently defends his project, defining the thin line between eco-tourism and philistine country-side resorts. "I won't deny that we don't like the money coming in but it is more important to us that we instill certain values in people who visit. Tamarind Tree invites school children every monsoon for rice cultivation," says Babu. There are also visitors from World Wide Opportunities for Organic farming (WWOOF), an organisation that began in the UK in 1971 and has facilitated the movement of organic farming enthusiasts across borders.

Initiatives in the direction have yielded a fresh crop of youngsters who have taken to organic farming. Twenty-five-year-old Varun Lulla, who has volunteered his services at the farm, is a documentary film-maker-turned-farmer. He is trying to develop his own piece of land on the outskirts of Pune. Ubai Husein, 27, visitor at Van Vadi, gave up a career as a chef in the US to try his hand at organic farming. He now grows a variety of fruits "and vegetables without much success" at his plot in Bhiwandi.

Archana Singh, who works closely with nutritionist Dr Vijaya Venkat has been running a four-acre farm at Wagani, on the Pune-Karjat route, not far from Badlapur. They organically grow several varieties of fruits and vegetable and keep their farm open to visitors who are free to use their large dormitory for relaxation (Rs 300 per day). "Visitors come to our farm for healthy food and a day off," she says. Archana runs her farm with husband Rajan and was initially offered four more acres to farm by the forest department. They denied the offer because the land was too large for them to manage.

Heading: New releases - Indian Express
Content:
MATTHEW HORROCKS
36, Film Producer

A secret you discovered about Mumbai?
Nothing special yet.

An Indian product or service you can't do without?
Bollywood movies: I've been addicted since I first saw Raja Hindustani. Cinephiles seem not to take this film so seriously—I loved it.

Any fashion tips?
I consider myself to be a walking fashion criminal. So I am not the one to give tips except to say to the women of this city shouldn't change a bit—you all look so glam.

Dared to try street food?
All the time. There's a place in Colaba behind the Taj Hotel I always like to go to. I did once suffer a night of 1000 years in Mumbai, but a street vendor wasn't to blame.

A phrase you're bound to hear?
"Mr Matthew. Have you ever thought of being in the movies? My cousin is a producer who is a good friend of Rakesh Roshan/Salman Khan/the Big B, who could help you."

Your road experiences?
Well my life is put each day in the hands of the rickshaw drivers of Mumbai. How concerned should I be? In another life, they'd all be Formula 1 racing drivers.

What is sexy about Mumbai?
Juhu beach.

Have you been conned yet?
Yes, in circumstances too embarrassing to recall, by an American who approached me at the Gateway of India.

Truly, madly, deeply, Mumbai...
Rahul da Cunha's Me Kash & Cruise at the Prithvi Theatre—three friends and 20 years of Mumbai history all in one play, it's terrific.

What are the similarities or differences between Mumbai and your hometown?
Like Mumbai, my hometown, Auckland, is also a blend of different cultures. The biggest difference: we have one million people, Mumbai has...how many?

Mumbai, the cultural capital?
Without doubt, an all-Indian city and a global one too. To paraphrase what a famous English writer said of London: "He who is tired of Mumbai is tired of life".

Heading: Derelict plots to make way for transit camps - Indian Express
Content:
Rebirth pangs
Karzzzz
When Subhash Ghai's Karz came out in 1980, there were mutterings about how it had ripped off the cheesy Hollywood drama The Reincarnation of Peter Proud. But they soon subsided not only because Ghai cleverly admitted to copying, having out-cheesed the original effortlessly. It was also because Karz was a cracker of an entertainer: as the born-again hero, Rishi rocked, there's never been a crueler, classier vamp than Simi Garewal, and if ever there is a compilation of classic movie themes, the haunting Ek Hasina Thi is sure to top the list.
This Karzzz, despite the extra Zs for luck, is a blot. Except for the names of the characters, which are exactly the same, nothing else is: the treatment is sloppy, even by Satish Kaushik's standards, and the acting is plain execrable.
For those who've come in 28 years after the fact, this is how it goes. Pop star Monty ( Himesh) starts having visions—of a man and a woman, a huge mansion in the hills, a kali ka mandir, and an airplane going up in flames. It's a case of punarjanam, a psychiatrist declares sagely. And whoosh, we are launched into a series of flashbacks, unraveling how Monty is actually rich businessman Ravi Varma ( Dino) re-incarnated, and has come into the world to wreak revenge on the murderous, greedy-for-his-millions-wife Kamini ( Urmila).
Himesh adds a hair transplant and a smile to his extremely-limited repertoire ( in his last year's debut Aap Ka Suroor, he had appeared throughout in his till-then trademark baseball cap, and scowl). A badly-made up Urmila dons skin-tight gowns, large tracts of her chest gleaming with bronzer, gold trousers, and scarlet lipstick. She also sounds distressingly like Archana Puran Singh when she simpers: hard to think that she was once an A-list actress. There's also a new girl, Shweta (director Indra Kumar's daughter) getting a brief look-see: all she has to do is to gaze adoringly at Himesh. That must have been tough.
Even the climactic song-cum-whodunit denouement, which has been lifted completely, is mangled. In between, you can hear Rohini Hattangadi, who plays the dukhiyari maa utter lines like these: mere kaleje ke tukda, she goes, mere laal.
Moral: if you can't make, don't re-make.

Shoot down
Shoot on Sight
JAG Mundhra's films have topical, relevant subjects. That's the good part. The bad part is that they do not possess a single subtle note: everything is heavily underscored, leaving no place for understatement or nuance.
And that's something one misses sorely, especially in a film like his latest. Shoot On Sight is based on the London bombings in 2005, which unleashed a whole spate of racial profiling. Is it a crime to be Muslim? Are all Muslims terrorists? These questions, asked by sundry characters in Shoot On Sight yield answers which, for all their truth, seem like they are stating the obvious.
It's not as if Naseer, as Commander Ali of Scotland Yard, doesn't know the pitfalls of playing a Muslim cop in a still-White country. In his scenes with 'gori' wife (Greta Scacchi), defiant daughter, couple of openly racist colleagues, and sympathetic boss (Brian), he shows as much deftness as the script allows. But that's not much at all: Ali's childhood friend from Lahore, now a mullah advocating jihad (Om) is all surface—he strokes his beard, recites from the Koran, and colours impressionable minds.
More predictabilities abound. Rebellious Muslim teenager facing off dad—he won't let her date white boys who want to go all the way. Jolly meat-shop owner doling out 'gosht' and good cheer. Good white wife trying to balance the tensions in her family, and his. We've seen all this before, with much more depth: there's more to multi-culturalism, and the problems of being brown, post 9/11, than these very broad, too familiar brush-strokes.
The Hindi dub flattens the film even more; catch the English version, if you have to.

Opportunity lost
Cheenti Cheenti Bang Bang
TWO colonies of ants live on either side of a river bank. Lal Cheentas and Kala Cheentas have presumably lived happily before the evil Ghun arrives in their midst, to sow dissent and discord.
This could have been a fun flick: ants, and other cute creepy-crawlies, lend themselves well to animation (Antz, A Bug's Life). Some money and effort have been spent on the production, but the characters are all cardboard, not being able to create the slightest interest in the proceedings.
What you get is endless, inane chatter peppered with creaky dialogue (nestanabood, yudhh ka danka baja diya, yunki baat ki baat hai, mere dil mein saadh hai). And an old ant called Lal Boodha who's supposed to have leered at a comely young thing, tells the ant queen: "woh mardood hamare badan pe toot pada".
Huh? This is supposed to be a film for little children?

SHUBHRA GUPTA

Terror talks
Body of Lies
RIDLEY Scott's Body of Lies raises a potentially disturbing question. If terrorism has become boring, does that mean the terrorists have won? Or, conversely, is the grinding tedium of this film good news for our side, evidence of the awesome might of Western popular culture, which can turn even the most bloodthirsty real-world villains into fodder for busy, contrived and lifeless action thrillers?
The second answer seems more plausible, but there are other puzzles in Body of Lies that are not so easily solved and that may distract from sober contemplation of geopolitical pseudo realities like Leonardo DiCaprio's accent or Russell Crowe's body mass index. DiCaprio, as CIA operative Roger Ferris, once again shows his commitment to full employment for dialect coaches, following Blood Diamond and The Departed, with some good-old-boy inflections that are helpfully identified by Crowe's character as originating in North Carolina.
Crowe, meanwhile, plays Ferris's supervisor, Ed Hoffman, who has no specified regional background to explain his odd drawl. At times Crowe, showing the linguistic chameleonism — the birthright of every Australian actor — spits out his words with an emphatic twanginess that suggests, if not George W Bush himself, then perhaps Jon Stewart impersonating Bush. It's possible that this resemblance is meant to imply their immunity to self-doubt and allergy to second thoughts about the righteousness of their actions.
Hoffman is fighting a war whose terms he lays out in a few set-piece speeches. The gist is that no one is innocent and that the ends justify the means. Deceit, torture, the sacrifice of non-American lives — all is permissible in the fight against a superjihadist Al-Saleem (Alon Aboutboul), carrying out suicide attacks around Europe. The contradictions and unintended consequences of Hoffman's tactics are borne by Ferris, who finds his credibility undermined, his friends and his life in danger.
All of which would be fine if Body of Lies—based on a novel by David Ignatius—was clearer about its themes or its plot. As it is, the movie is a hodgepodge of borrowings and half-cooked ideas, flung together into a feverishly edited jet-setting exercise in purposeless intensity.

AO SCOTT/NYT

Heading: BMC solution to parking overcharge: Prepaid card - Indian Express
Content:
Their original occupants already in camps, they'll now house residents of run-down buildings in need of relocation

For decades these tiny plots, with only rubble or empty structures on them, have been of little use other than serve as a metaphor for the problems that plague the 19,000 dilapidated structures in the island city. Now, 110 such plots will be used to construct transit camps for residents of old and run-down buildings that pay a repair cess.

The original residents of these buildings have been languishing in transit camps for years after their structure either gave way or was declared too derelict to live in. Usually the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) takes the responsibility of reconstructing such structures. Most of these buildings are over a century old, built much before the Development Control Rules came into force and hence are on extremely narrow plots, cheek by jowl with neighbouring buildings.

"As per the DC rules, it is mandatory for all new constructions to leave an open space of 10 feet on all four sides. Since these plots are too small, the buildings could never be reconstructed," said VG Vani, Executive Engineer of MHADA's Repair Board. The BMC, he added, has agreed to allow transit camps on the plots after condoning the open space restrictions as transit camps are temporary by definition, though not really so in practice.

MHADA's existing transit tenements have been around since the time they were first constructed: some 20,000 rooms spread over 56 locations. Of this, barely 5,400 rooms are in the island city and the rest are in the suburbs.

"Tenants from old or collapsed structures have to face dislocation to a great extent due to the dearth of transit accommodation in the island city. This is why we decided to make use of these plots. This may be a long drawn process as we have to still acquire these from landlords," said MHADA Chief Engineer D Haddare. He said that tenants who were earlier occupants of these plots would be given a choice between shifting to the new 225 sq ft tenements constructed on these plots or continuing to live in transit camps they have been in for years.

The open space concession for transit camps would mean that the built-up and plot area of these structures will be the same as that of the original building, a potential hazard in case of a fire or building collapses. Said Haddare, "In case at a later stage the adjoining buildings want to go in for redevelopment under the proposed cluster redevelopment scheme, the transit camps could also be reconstructed by adhering to the open space regulations."

Heading: ED opposes Rajan wife’s plea for permission to travel abroad - Indian Express
Content:
Move follows complaints of fleecing by private contractors

People parking their vehicles at the city's 100-odd pay-and-park facilities can now look forward to not getting duped by parking contractors. Instead of worrying about being overcharged or getting into arguments with the attendants, they can soon swipe a prepaid card at computerised terminals and pay for parking their vehicles.

The move by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation to introduce such cards that can be used at computerised parking metres follows complaints by people using pay-and-park facilities that they were being fleeced by the contractors.

"There is certain grey area and discrepancies in the contractor system. Through pre-paid cards, parking charges will be calculated automatically for the exact time the vehicle was parked. Contractors will not be required and the pocketing of money will be done away with," said Additional Municipal Commissioner (City) R A Rajeev.

The computerised metres will be installed at pay-and-park facilities which are at present run by private agencies who got contracts from the BMC. The contractors collect charges on behalf of the civic body from people who park their vehicles. Commuters are often known to be overcharged in the absence of a rate-list by the BMC at the facility. "The pre-paid parking metres will encourage transparency as there will be no middlemen involved," said Deputy Chief Traffic Engineer, P Desai.

Prepaid parking metres are commonly used across many countries. Drivers entering a parking area get a card when they push a button, which contains information of the date and time at which the card was taken. Drivers carry the card with them and during their exit, swipe it through a slot to get a receipt with details of the duration they had parked and the charges.

The civic body plans to study the feasibility of the project and will introduce it on an experimental basis at select pay-and-park facilities.

The BMC has invited Expressions of Interest and has asked companies to suggest the best technology to implement the system. The system will be replicated across the city after the pilot project is successful, officials said.

Heading: To bring more children to its schools, BMC introduces magnetic boards - Indian Express
Content:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has opposed the application by fugitive gangster Chhota Rajan's wife, Sujata Nikhalje, for permission to travel abroad to help admit her daughter in a foreign university, saying that the investigation against Nikhalje under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act was in the final stage.

The ED, which is also investigating the assets of Nikhalje, moved an application in the special court on Saturday opposing her petition to travel abroad and also defreeze her bank account to help fund her daughter's education.

The investigation "is in the process of finalisation" and Nikhalje may be required to be present in India "for smooth proceedings", said the ED's Assistant Director, A P Bandekar. The ED application also seeks that along with Nikhalje's bank account and financial transactions, assets in her children's name also be scanned.

Nikhalje was granted bail by the MCOCA court last year after she was arrested in 2005 on charges of being a part of an organised crime syndicate run by her husband. The Crime Branch of Mumbai police alleged that she was threatening builders and residents of the Tilak Nagar area where the family lives to corner a major share of redevelopment projects for her own firm.

Earlier this month, Nikhalje sought permission from the special court to travel to Hong Kong and Singapore as she wanted to escort her daughter, Anita, for securing admissions in universities there. She said Anita had earlier got through to colleges in Britain and Australia to do a BSc in psychology but could not go as she had no one to accompany her to complete the admission process. She has also applied to institutions in Singapore and Hong Kong and is expected to get through next month, her mother's petition says.

Heading: Forest land: Residents want ‘illegal’ tag off, CM gives them hope - Indian Express
Content:
Keeping in mind the high dropout ratio, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) is all set to improve the infrastructure in civic schools as they hope this will bring more children to these schools. As part of this initiative, the civic body has installed magnetic green boards at schools in F-ward.

"It's a pilot project which we started in December last year. We have installed these boards in municipal schools in the F-ward. We hope that these boards will improve the condition of civic schools. This is one of the moves to attract more children to civic schools," said Ujwala Modak, chairperson of the education committee.

In last year's budget, the BMC had decided to substantially boost its education and health departments. The civic body had found that many of municipal schools across the city were in precarious condition and had set aside Rs 1,253 crore for the development of these schools. Installation of magnetic green boards are part of this plan.

According to the sources, at present, the civic body has installed magnetic boards measuring 4X6 sq ft in 150 classrooms in F-ward schools and each of these boards costs Rs 15,500, nearly Rs 13,000 more than the cost of ordinary blackboards.

"It has been scientifically proven that these boards are children-friendly. The green colour makes these boards non-reflective and it's pleasing to the eyes. The magnet helps the duster stick on the boards easily. Also, these boards come with a tray attached to it. This helps in free-flow of chalk particles. All these factors make these boards user-friendly," said Deputy Education Officer Sukhada Lad. "Chalk markings will be clearer on these boards," she said.

The green magnetic boards are made of fibre glass which gives a smooth finishing and clarity. "Since, it is made of fibre glass, it is strong and will not develop cracks. The traditional blackboard is more fragile. It's also not very heavy and hence can be easily moved," said Lad. Though education officials claimed that teachers and children had responded well to the installation of these magnetic boards, some teachers opined that it was not a very big deal. "These magnetic boards have a smooth finish which makes it easier to rub. Secondly, the duster sticks to it. But these are the only plus points. I don't see it as a major change," said a teacher of the Prabhodhan Thackeray Kreedangana Marathi School at Sewree on condition of anonymity. In this school, nine classrooms have got such boards. "Our school won the model school award last year. Magnetic green boards are another feather in our cap. They have made life easier for teachers and students alike. Now, we hope it will get us more students too," said Raghunath Shirvadekar, a teacher of the same school.

The civic body will soon be replicating this model in other wards too. "We have seen a good response from teachers and students of F-ward schools. By this year end, we will install such boards in 8,500 class rooms across Mumbai. We hope that these measures will increase the number of students in civic schools," said Lad.

Heading: In Gurgaon, woman held for killing nephew, 6 - Indian Express
Content:
For nearly 20 lakh residents in the eastern and western suburbs of Mumbai, shaking off the tag of 'illegal residents in reserved forest lands' seems to be getting daunting by the day. However, their meeting with Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh on Friday has given them reason to be hopeful.

Responding to an application filed by the state Forest Department in the Supreme Court on September 28, several aggrieved residents along with NGOs from the suburbs met the CM, and requested amendments to the schemes mentioned in the affidavit. In a letter submitted to the CM's office, representative of Mulund-based NGOs — People's Power of Nation (PPN) and Hillside Resident's Welfare Association (HRWA)— stated that "the scheme given in the application for the affected people is not justified to all".

As per the application, the forest department has pleaded that the lands put to non-forestry use before October 25, 198— coming under the Maharashtra Private Forest (Acquisition) Act of 1975 and having all the approvals of the government "be treated as deleted from the category of forests", and non-forestry activity be allowed on them without any afforestation charges. However, for the residents of buildings constructed after 1980 (up to 2006) it appeals that such lands should be deemed "restored land" and "only charges for afforesting equivalent forest lands be collected" from them.

Anmol Bhushan, president of PPN, said the affidavit seemed to be biased. "This affidavit does not display parity between residents and builders. According to it, most commercial construction would be exempted without any fine while residents, who purchased flats lawfully, have to live under the title of 'restored lands' despite paying afforestation fees," Bhushan said, adding, "We want the same relief as given to construction done before 1980." The NGOs' letter stated that "the title of 'restored lands' may invite some restrictions as the plots may remain private forest lands as per some earlier Supreme Court orders".

According to the affidavit, commercial complexes like Nirmal Lifestyles, several Runwal constructions, etc., would be cleared of the forest land title, but lands of people living in populated residential areas like Ghodbunder Road, Malad, Mulund, etc. would have 'restored forest lands' status.

However, residents are hopeful for a favourable solution. Prakash Paddikal, president to HRWA, said: "The CM's office on Friday clearly told the forest department to prepare an additional application to support the residents. We have no problem with afforestation fees as long as we are relieved from the 'illegal residents' tag." Rajendra Munglurkar, deputy secretary (revenue and forests), said: "We have been instructed by the CM to make an additional application seeking further concession for the residents. Concessions for non-forestry work done before and after 1980 cannot be same, but we have taken into account the people's welfare and have made several concessions. We believe that all their demands will be granted."

Meanwhile, the affidavit stated that the residents with construction after 2006 would have to pay afforestation charges 10 times the current value.

Heading: Babus spar, HC judges ‘homeless’ - Indian Express
Content:
A 23-year-old woman was arrested on Friday evening from Tigra village here on charges of killing her nephew, six years old.

Bodies of three of her other nephews were also found from her room last year, and though the family had not smelled foulplay at the time and thus did not approach the police, the cops are investigating those cases as well.

The police on Saturday said the accused, Babita, has admitted killing the child, though they are still not clear about the motive.

The incident came to light on October 11, when six-year-old Sunny, who had gone missing the previous day, was found dead from Babita's room. The boy's father, Ajit Singh, had filed a missing complaint with Sadar police on October 10. And though Singh now claims he had seen strangulation marks on his son's body, the family did not suspect any foulplay at the time; they had cremated him without a postmortem being conducted.

Singh, however, lodged an FIR after Babita seemingly remained "unmoved" with the death — she, in fact, behaved "very normally", many villagers alleged. "She did not attend the last rites of my son — her own nephew — and shed no tears even though my child was very attached to her," Singh alleged.

Two of Babita's brothers, Subhash and Veeda, have also been named in the FIR.

The case, though, seemed to have opened a Pandora's box for the Singh family, as three children from the family were found dead last year in Babita's room; in eerily similar manner, says the family. Gaurav, 2, one-and-a-half years old Saurabh, and Preeti, 5, were found dead within a span of five months. But like in Sunny's case last week, the family did not suspect foul play.

According to Singh, they believed black magic – "evil" – had caused the trio's death.

And, again like in Sunny's case, their last rites were performed without any postmortem.

"We are not clear whether she (Babita) has a role to play in the previous three deaths; we are investigating," the SHO of Sadar police station said. "She has been difficult and is not divulging details. We have sent some evidence for forensic tests and are waiting for the reports.

"The biggest drawback in the case is that no postmortem was done when Sunny's body was found."

The extended family lives together and Ajit Singh said there has till date been no dispute — over property or otherwise — among the brothers. "We live in the same compound, the three of us brothers. Gopal (Babita's husband) is our first cousin," Singh said. "We have never had any fight amongst ourselves."

He said Gopal and Babita were married four years ago and the couple has a one-and-a-half-year-old daughter.

Police ruled out the possibility that the accused could have committed the crime/crimes under any sort of psychological disorder. "She is absolutely in her senses and it is highly unlikely that any such possibility could crop up," the SHO said. Babita has been sent to three days of police remand.

Heading: Two years after ‘fake encounter’, victims’ kin get relief: Rs 3 lakh - Indian Express
Content:
UD ministry says no spare bungalow, Delhi govt says no land. So who will house the judges?

The Urban Development Ministry and the Delhi government has had a series of collisions of late over Commonwealth Games and infrastructure projects. And the latest bone of contention is providing residential accommodation for Delhi High Court judges. While the ministry says its responsibility is limited to providing accommodation to only Supreme Court judges, the Delhi government has passed the issue forward due to "lack of bungalows and land".

According to the High Court Judges Rules, 1956 (as on January 1, 2007), a High Court judge is entitled to several benefits, including an official residence, throughout the term of office and an additional month and furnishings for the house up to a limit of Rs 1.5 lakh. For the HC Chief Justice, the ceiling on furnishing is up to Rs 2 lakh. The benefits also include free water upto 3,600 kilolitres and power of up to 10,000 units anually.

In case of rented accommodation, the government pays the rent.

But now, while Supreme Court judges get bungalows from the Centre - the Ministry of Urban Development, to be precise - and judges of the five lower courts in the city are provided accommodation in the form of apartments by the Delhi government through its general pool of accommodation in Shahdara, Dwarka and Gulabi Bagh, High Court judges have missed the bus. "One big problem is that the number of High Court judges has risen and we simply do not have enough bungalows to accommodate them. So we have asked the Delhi government to provide accommodation as it is the state's responsibility to take care of its judges," Secretary (Urban Development) M Ramachandran told Newsline.

The number of High Court judges has increased from 30 to 42 in the last six months. Officials said the number is likely to go up further.

"The problem is we cannot accommodate High Court judges through the general pool," Delhi Chief Secretary Rakesh Mehta said. "They have to be given bungalows and we simply do not have any. There are a couple of vacant bungalows but these have been allocated to Delhi government ministers; it is up to them whether they use them (but) they cannot be reallocated.

"We have told the ministry to give us land and we will be more than willing to construct new bungalows. But that proposal has been turned down."

A member of the Delhi Bar Association said housing for HC judges has been an issue for some time now. "None of the new appointees have received accommodation," the member, who does not want to be named, said. "There was a proposal in the ministry to give High Court judges land in Chanakyapuri but this has now been shot down."

Heading: Financial crisis drove NCR executive to suicide: cops - Indian Express
Content:
Two years after two Ghaziabad-based men were killed in a fake encounter at Timarpur, their families have been granted compensation of Rs 3 lakh each following directions from the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC).

Nazakat, a labourer, and Zulfiqar, a taxi driver, lived in Hawalpur, Ghaziabad. They were gunned down by Delhi Police in an encounter on July 31, 2006.

Ghaziabad police registered an FIR after relatives of the deceased protested their killing. The case was later transferred to the Crime Branch and it was found by their investigations and postmortem reports that the encounter was fake. The probe found the policemen conducted it to avenge the death of a fellow policeman's brother. Nine policemen were dismissed subsequently.

Now, ACO (North district) has written to DCP (Headquarters) seeking details of relatives of the two men killed for issuing the cheques bearing interim relief of Rs 3 lakhs each. The letter, dated September 17, says, "The head of accounts, under which the payment is to be made, may also be intimated to this office for taking appropriate action."

Deceased Zulfiqar's father Ghulam Nabi told Newsline the family didn't even know they were eligible for compensation, but "some policemen guided us". He said the family members were called to the Delhi Police Headquarters last month and given the letter detailing the compensation.

"My son was the family's only earning member and I am working as a scrap dealer in Delhi since his death," Nabi said. "The compensation would not, of course, get my son back but at least I can get my other children married off with the money."

Zulfiqar's wife, he added, is living with her parents for the past year. The couple had two children.

Babu, father of the fake encounter's other victim Nazakat, said the family had as good as given up hope of ever getting the compensation and "actually surprised" when they got the confirmation that about the Rs 3-lakh amount.

Ghulam Nabi's brother-in-law Irfan said, "I have seen Ghulam running from pillar to post to feed his family after the so-called encounter took away his eldest son. He has fought every day for his family's survival."

Ghulam Nabi's family includes his wife, four sons and two daughters.

Nabi also expressed his "gratitude" towards Ghaziabad police personnel: "After all, they heard my plea and registered a case against their Delhi counterparts."

Meanwhile, with Pramod Kumar Tyagi, one of the accused policemen, still at large, Ghulam Nabi says they are still living in fear. "Though we have not been able to confirm this, recently we got information that he has escaped to the US."

Heading: Now under the hammer: art by animals - Indian Express
Content:
Neighbours say US supermarket Macy's recently turned down a huge consignment from Bhadwal's firm, which worsened the family's crisis

The police drew a blank a day after Vikram Bhadwal, a Gurgaon-based senior executive with an export house, committed suicide early Friday morning.

A day on, Ridgewood Estate, an upmarket housing society with over 900 flats and thousands of residents, seemed to have regained a semblance of normalcy after Bhadwal allegedly jumped off his 11th-floor apartment's bathroom window. Though neighbours remain reticent about the 47-year-old, they believe he took the step due to a severe financial crisis.

Even the police believe an acute financial crisis was the reason behind Bhadwal's suicide. His father Krishna Kumar, a retired Air Force officer who lives with his wife at Princeton State in Gurgaon, has reportedly confirmed to the police that the family was undergoing financial crisis.

Bhadwal was a quality control expert at Macy's Buying House in Okhla Phase-I in South Delhi. A neighbour today said a major consignment at Bhadwal's company had to deliver to Macy was cancelled recently. According to the neighbour, the ongoing recession in the United States could be the reason behind the consignment being cancelled, and that could have fuelled further financial crisis for the family.

Kittu Mathur, the apartment complex's secretary, said the family had moved in four or five years ago and were warm and friendly. "The husband-wife duo had set up a stall in the society on Thursday evening as part of the Karva Chauth mela," Mathur said. "Vikram was proactive in RWA meetings and the couple seemed to be happy.

"When I met Vikram's wife Richa after the tragedy, all she asked amid tears was a 'why?'."

The couple has an eight-year-old daughter, Gayatri.

Newsline called the family from the building's intercom but they refused to meet anyone or clarify any facts.

Heading: Plans and strategies: Congress keeps cards close to chest - Indian Express
Content:
Rani and Ramkali's artwork in edible vegetable dyes will show at an art auction on Sunday. So what's big, you ask? Rani is a bear, and Ramkali an elephant, that's what.

While Rani has used her paws in the painting, Ramkali's foot, latticed with depressions from walking on hot, tarred city roads, presents a coloured paw impression — a unique art in its own right.

The frames would be part of an auction at the French Embassy on Sunday. The art auction 'India on Canvas', an annual event, is organised by the NGO Khushii.

The sloth bears and Indian elephants, whose 'paintings' are part of the auction, have been rescued by the NGO Wildlife SOS. Professional artists have woven paintings around paw and trunk impressions by the animals, and five of these will be part of the auction.

The proceeds will go to fund conservation efforts.

"This is an effort to create an out of the ordinary art piece as well as highlight the cause of the sloth bear and the elephant India," says Kartick Satyanarayan, co-founder, Wildlife SOS.

"Sloth bears who have created the painting have been rescued from 'kalandars', who used them as dancing bears. The elephants are working animals whose cause we want to highlight," he says.

"By raising money through this cause, we can actually buy the elephants away from a life of hard work."

While paintings co-made by animals, especially elephants, are a common tool for conservation abroad, the concept is still new in India. For Khushii, including 'animal artists' is a first.

"We hold 'India on Canvas' each year but this is the first time we are including paintings by animals. This is a very new and interesting concept and we are hopeful it would be a success," says Prina Mitra of Khushii.

Heading: Out with the past - Indian Express
Content:
Both the Congress and the BJP are busy trying to come up with something innovative to attract voters.

For both parties, it will be a tough task to get voters out of their houses. Even in the MCD polls last year the voter turnout was merely 30 per cent.

At a time when public rallies are a passé, Delhi BJP is planning to launch a website soon, while the Congress will set up a campaigning control room in each district.

The BJP has elaborate plans for the elections, in the backyard of the Delhi BJP office. Workers are busy building makeshift cabins for various election committees being formed at present. On Saturday too, party leaders organised various meetings with IT firms.

"We are at present planning to install equipments which can transmit speeches of our leaders to the neighbouring area using bluetooth. So whenever there is a public rally, even the people do not come to the venue will be able to hear the speech," said a senior BJP leader.

The BJP will also be using their timetested measure of calling up voters and relaying a pre-recorded message. Through these pre-recorded messages, the chief ministerial candidate Vijay Malhotra will reach out to voters directly. Several lakh SMSes asking for votes would also be sent out.

Television advertisements will soon start coming out, but the political parties do not yet have a nod from the Election Commission for campaigning on radio. "We will be brainstorming and the most cost-effective methods will be utilised," said Delhi BJP president, Dr Harshvardhan.

The Congress, meanwhile, in a tougher spot facing the anti-incumbency factor, are not revealing their cards. "We will be setting up control rooms in each district which will closely monitor campaigning in each constituency. This control room will be directly connected to one in Delhi Pradesh Congress office where senior leaders will be able monitor it directly," said Congress MLA Subhas Chopra who is also heading the Congress election campaigning committee.

Heading: JNU: Nominations over, parties declare candidates - Indian Express
Content:
Author of Memories of a Gay Life, Sunil Gupta, revisits Jamali Kamali, a tomb he calls significant for the Indian gay community

It's a breezy morning at the imposing monument Jamali Kamali, nestled deep inside Mehrauli. Strolling past the mosque, photographer Sunil Gupta, 55, points out verses inscribed on the walls, composed by Jamal Khan, the Sufi saint whom the tomb is named after. Kamali's identity remains a mystery. "This tomb is significant for the Indian gay community," says Gupta. "We regard it as India's only gay monument."

Gupta has used one symbolic image of Jamali Kamali for his book Memories of a Gay Life, a deeply personal visual account tracing his own journey on coming out as a gay Indian. In a career spanning over 25 years, most of Gupta's work in photography revolves around issues of identity and the ongoing debate on homosexuality. He currently has an exhibit 'Street Portraits', shot in Delhi on display at the Tate Museum in London and most of his work is priced upwards of 7000 pounds. After living in Montreal and London where he studied photography, Gupta moved to Delhi in 2004 stating wryly, that he moved for a man. "Unfortunately, that didn't work out. But I was pleasantly surprised to see a big change among gay people here. In the '70s there was so much hypocrisy. Now at least there is a small bunch of us who are out," says Gupta.

Memories of a Gay Life is mostly autobiographical and shows Gupta in moments with friends, lovers and colleagues from around the globe. Gupta gently provokes with some brutally honest images of himself when he discovered he was HIV+ in 1995. A thread of quiet angst runs through the visuals, fiercely original and brave in their candour. Gupta says the human situation and his own emotional life are the endearing themes in his work. In one exhibit shown abroad, 'Love and Light', Gupta describes shooting his then companion in Ladakh, nude, with the Himalayas as the backdrop. "There are few personal stories emerging from India in photography," says Gupta, currently documenting his own love life after HIV for a New York museum. A keen observer of India's gay movement, Gupta is confident there will be dramatic changes in Article 377 that currently criminalizes homosexuality. "Everywhere the attitude to homosexuality is changing. It will percolate here too," says Gupta, though he is sceptical of the idea of gay marriage. "It's an institution that's barely surviving in the heterosexual world," he says. Gupta has another show coming up at the Vadehra Art Gallery next September, again on gay love. As we stroll into the small chamber of the twin tombs at Jamali Kamali, where the ceiling is decorated with coloured, intricate frescoes, Gupta says with a twinkle, "There's hope yet."

Memories of a Gay Life is published by Yoda Press. Price: Rs 995

Heading: The show goes on - Indian Express
Content:
Friday being the last day of filing nominations, student bodies of Jawaharlal Nehru University on Saturday spent most of their time preparing their list of candidates for 35 posts. Sandeep Singh, the existing President of JNUSU for AISA will be fighting the elections again while SFI has pitted Roshan Kishore against him.

Sandeep says his candidature was purely a party decision and if he comes to power, he will continue involving students with world affairs. "My opponents say that I focus on world affairs rather then college issues but I feel in today's world everything in inter-connected," he said.

Both Youth for Equality (YFE) and NSUI have refused to confirm its candidates but sources say Faiz Ashrafi will be fighting for the post of the president for the latter. YFE says they will confirm their candidates by Sunday. The party is confident that after being the second most popular party last year, they have good chances of making it to the panel this year.

"We have the most number of councillors in the university and the prospects look good," said a party member.

Till Friday, a total of 390 candidates had filed their nominations for the entire council. Around 10 candidates of Akhil Bhartiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) have filed their nominations for the posts of president, vice-president, joint secretary and secretary.

From other Right-wing students' union NSUI, nine students have filed their nominations.

Around seven students filed nominations from the platform of the ultra Left wing students' organisation AISA, that was the winner of all the four seats last year.

The candidates can withdraw their nominations on 19 October and final list of the candidates will be displayed on 20 October.

Heading: Students across the country display models at CBSE national science meet - Indian Express
Content:
It no longer draws crowds but it's not ready to quit yet. Shoba V takes a ringside view of the Apollo Circus in Noida

First, it's three balls, then rings, and then sticks, all flung up in the air in quick succession, each throw at a calculated velocity, the objects landing to perch, bird-like, in the juggler's palm one by one. Most seats at the Apollo Circus are unoccupied, but the modest audience hardly takes its eyes off the stage. A few metres from where the tent is pitched—in Sector 25, Noida—people throng the cool retreat of the PVR Spice Mall, checking out retail kitsch and catching the latest multiplex release. Once a pop-cultural phenomenon, the circus is now a rarefied art of impossible stunts, daredevilry and funny fillers.

The scale and grandeur are noticeably watered down, but the spirit is intact. With the ban on training lions and bears for the circus, other—more tame—animals are the stars of the show. Dangling from the trunk of an elephant—which stands on all fours on a perilously tiny stool—a girl in a bodysuit twirls to generous applause. Little dogs roll over and skip when a young trainer pats them gently with a stick. There are horses too, and a three-legged goat, paraded round the circular platform to the beat of drums and the familiar tune of a Rishi Kapoor song, a tune that belongs to another era, like the circus itself. The drummer and the musician are seated on a platform above, with a good view of the stage. So when the clowns saunter up, they know it's time to stop playing.

The dwarf clown chats up a boy dressed in striped pajamas. The dwarf produces three items and counts them again and again, adding them up to 10. To which the boy retorts that he can do better. He proceeds to count till 10, just like the dwarf did, and knocks him out with a slap, saying that's 11. Another clown launches into a schmaltzy song, and gets all the lyrics messed up. Peals of laughter echo in the canvas tent. Anticipation of the next act hangs in the air like some faint perfume. Sure enough, the following trapeze act leaves everyone breathless. For a moment, the golden age of live family entertainment seems to be back.

A waif-thin girl plays with a rope and hula-hoops; another coaxes cockatoos to jump hurdles and ride a tiny cycle. Yet others do choreographed routines and climb up on one another's shoulders. Two young women balance themselves on platforms placed on cylindrical barrels and juggle sticks with one end on fire. A tightrope walker in a waistcoat glugs down a bottle of what looks like liquor and steadies herself with casual deliberation.

Suddenly, heads turn as two motorbikes vroom inside a metal globe, accelerating to a speed that can shatter the riders' skulls should they bump into each other. Yet, for all the thrills, the circus wears a desolate look. The outfits are jaded, and sometimes a wan smile escapes from an artiste's lips-artistes are paid anything between Rs 2,000 and Rs 10,000. The chips and ice cream sellers walk about with their trays full and their pockets empty. Amit complains, "Aaj kal bachche TV dekhna pasand karte hain, circus kaun aata hai? (These days, kids prefer watching TV, who comes to the circus?)" It's a concern shared by Apollo Circus General Manager R.K. Yadav. We have 80 artistes and 250 staff members. The cost of running a circus is Rs 30,000 per day. We manage to recover it on weekends, but not every day. The government should promote circus troupes," he says.

Heading: Man killed in Blueline accident - Indian Express
Content:
Young Scientists of India presented their models "for the future" at the 5th CBSE National Level Science Exhibition on Saturday.

Hosted by Springdales School, Pusa Road the exhibition saw the participation of 178 schools from across the country, chosen for the best display in their respective regions by the CBSE.
