The themes for the competition include water management, disaster management, energy, food and agriculture, mathematical modelling and educational aides. The 20 best exhibits will receive awards from the CBSE.

"This kind of exposure helps develop a scientific temper among school students because they have to do a lot of research to develop their ideas," Himanshu Agrawal, of Lovedale School in Satna, Madhya Pradesh, said.

His student prepared a model on the application of genetic engineering technology to develop high-nutrition, low-priced foods.

The models on display ranged from dome shaped earthquake resistant buildings to biotechnology experiments carried out by the students themselves.

A particularly interesting exhibit revolved around using chemicals derived from moss to fight food contamination.

A competition on this scale is also an opportunity to interact with like-minded students from across the country and to learn from their work.

"We get to meet so many new people and see what others are doing in different fields," Priya Sehgal of Springdale Secondary School, Ludhiana, said.

She displayed a model on better methods of irrigation to save water.

Amita M Wattal, principal of the host school, emphasised the importance of holding such competitions as an outlet for creativity. "This is a brilliant way to make sure that children imbibe what they are learning,' she said, adding, "At a time when people source information from the Internet, this encourages thorough research and logical thinking."

A K Rath, Secretary of Department of School Education, MHRD, inaugurated the exhibition, which is open till Sunday evening.

Heading: Man held for attack on mediapersons in Jamia Nagar - Indian Express
Content: A 35-year-old died while another suffered severe injuries after the motorcycle they were travelling on was hit by a speeding Blueline bus in Govindpuri area of south-east district on Saturday. According to the police, the incident took place around 5:30 pm when two persons on a bike were hit by a Blueline bus plying on route no 511 (Dhaula Kuan and Badarpur border) from behind. Both received critical injuries. The duo was taken to a nearby hospital where one of them, Bala Ram, was declared brought dead by doctors while another person is still admitted in the All India Institute of Medical Sciences. After the incident, the bus driver fled the spot leaving the bus behind. However, he was later arrested and a case of rash and negligent driving registered against him at Govindpuri police station. Bala Ram used to work as a private contractor.

Heading: Delhi’s Water Front - Indian Express
Content:
One person was arrested for being part of the mob that allegedly beat up mediapersons in Batla House area in Jamia Nagar on Friday. A senior police officer said one Azhar was arrested in connection with the assault on journalists on Friday night.

Another person involved in the assault has been identified as Amanatullaha and would be arrested soon, said the police.

Two journalists and a cameraman of a news channel were injured when a mob attacked mediapersons during SP leader Amar Singh's visit to Jamia. A cameraman of Sahara Samay NCR, Afzal, was seriously injured while correspondents of a channel, Mahua and Asif and Star News journalist, Javed, were also injured.

Police arrested Azhar on the basis of the complaint filed by Asif. On Friday, the General Secretary of Samajwadi Party, Amar Singh had come to the area to meet a local leader and discuss the encounter in which two alleged terrorists were shot last month.

The mob angered by the questions posed by journalists allegedly beat up a few of them. According to the police, the situation turned ugly when mediapersons tried to ask Amar Singh a few questions. According to eyewitness Abdul, "Some people forcibly stopped journalists from talking to the leader and assaulted them on the spot. At the beginning of the meeting too a few locals tried to stop journalists. Confirming the arrest, the Deputy Commissioner of Police (Southeast district), Ajay Chaudhary said, "Azhar has been arrested and those who are absconding will be arrested soon."

Heading: Refugees in Delhi:  ‘Fewer chances of subsistence, jobs’ - Indian Express
Content:
A group of citizens sets up a website campaigning for clean drinking water

Buying jars of mineral water in the absence of a clean water supply was burning a hole in Mousumi Roy's pocket. She decided to do something about it. Getting together with a few friends and with the help of her techie-husband, Roy set up delhiforwater.com four months ago.

"The water we got at home was so brackish we could not even wash clothes or clean our utensils with it. Our pleas to the authorities fell on deaf ears," says Roy, 37, an economist. The website is a signature campaign to convince the state government to give Delhi's residents better water. "So far 17 people have signed up on the website. It may be a small number but we are speaking to various environmentalists and experts on this issue," says Roy. One of the members of the group, Purnendu Bhattacharya, 44, a housing-expert working with a Dutch firm, joined this group to express as a concerned Delhiite. "I feel having lakes around Delhi would be a permanent solution to the problem of water shortage," says Bhattacharya.

The group has come up with some suggestions: setting up two de-salination plants that can pump sea water into the city, creating four lakes around Delhi in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana which can hold 4,000 cusecs each, absorption of sea water into the swamp lands and grasslands in the existing ridge areas and making rain water harvesting compulsory. "If we set up de-salination plants in Delhi, at least we can be assured of clean water from the sea," she says.

The group acknowledges that since they are not experts not all solutions would be workable. "Some solutions may seem practical, others might not. We are looking for the best possible way out of this mess," she adds.

The group is also looking at other countries to replicate their solutions. For instance, in South Africa, Johannesburg has set up many water treatment plants. "After we get a decent response, we will be able to convince the authorities into taking some action. At the moment we are in talks with The Energy Resources Institute (TERI) and Mumbai-based water treatment company, Thermax, to sponsor our website," says Roy.

Heading: Lok Adalat strikes right chord with litigants - Indian Express
Content:
Asef has a degree in engineering from the Polytechnic University in Kabul and had a good life back home. A refugee now, he ekes out a living by supplying food to restaurants and can barely make ends meet.

After the Taliban took over, Asef had to flee in 2006. But for the 38-year-old, his trails were far from over. Because the Indian government doesn't provide refugees with residence allowance or a work permit, Asef's problems have only mounted in the last couple of years.

Aaisha, Asef's wife, who has a bachelor's in English Literature, says: "We had to flee Afghanistan because we felt insecure. We were in danger. But in New Delhi, we have found fewer chances of subsistence and employment."

Providing refuge for 25 years
Thousands of Afghan nationals have sought refuge in India over the last 25 years. Among them a majority are Sikh and Hindu refugees. About 200 of these have become naturalised citizens of India. But for the ethnic Afghans, the road is a long one. The culture is different and there are language barriers, and they want to be resettled elsewhere, a United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) official says.

Want to go home but can't
Ali (26), also escaped from Afghanistan. "Rebels beheaded my brother in 2007. I had no choice but to flee and seek asylum here," he says. "But I'm absolutely shocked at my circumstances." He used to be a professional kick boxer and won the Asian Kickboxing Competition in Dubai in 2004. He also won a bronze medal in the International Kickboxing Competition in India the same year. Ali now works in a car workshop in Delhi and earns Rs 1,500 a month. He can't afford rented accommodation and sleeps in the workshop, he said.
Many Afghan refugees, who are now vendors or hawkers in the city, held prominent positions in Afghanistan before they were forced to leave. Some returned to Afghanistan only to sneak into India once again. Conditions back home are still unstable, they say.
Perkashkor (35), mother of three, came to Delhi during the Taliban regime. After her husband abandoned her recently, she was forced to look for odd jobs in order to provide for her family. "I really want to go back. But due to insecurity there, I can't," she says.
After the UNHCR reduced monetary assistance for Afghan refugees in 1998, thousands were impoverished and driven into debt. The Indian government's failure to provide aid added to the woes of the refugees, who are concentrated in parts of West Delhi and near Nizamuddin Basti, where a lot of Muslim refugees, including Bangladeshis, live.

Laminated piece of hope
Iraqi refugee Rafed Kadhim's identity is a laminated blue sheet of paper given to him by the UNHCR that states he is a recognised refugee, which he always carries with him. No protection against detention for being illegally present in India, the paper, Kadhim hopes, will at least establish him as somebody ¿ a vulnerable Iraqi refugee who has nowhere to go.
He fled Iraq with his family in 2006 after some of his relatives were killed by extremists for allegedly helping American soldiers.
The family sold ice blocks to the Iraqi and American armies in Baghdad, where they owned a factory. When their unit was burned down by extremists and he was labelled a traitor, the family fled to neighbouring Syria and then Jordan, but with no visas they could not stay in these countries for long. The family then came to India, hoping the UNHCR will help them settle somewhere finally.
But the wait has only begun.
In a crammed one-bedroom tenement that Kadhim shares with his wife and three children in Krishna Nagar, the family has been marking days off the calendar. It has been two years already. Another 99 Iraqi refugees are also waiting for the UNHCR to make a decision.
"They tell me to wait. I am afraid for my family," he says. The blue paper, which allows only for temporary stay in India, is renewed every 18 months.
A UNHCR official said the paper, though not a legal permit recognised by the Indian government, is respected by officials aInd so far no cases of harassment or exploitation have been reported. The paper, however, can't get Kadhim a job or a decent apartment.
At first, he sold his laptop, then his wife sold all her gold jewellery, and then they pawned little things to stay afloat. The UNHCR's subsistence allowance of Rs 4,600 is just enough to pay the rent.
Like most Iraqi refugees living in the area, Kadhim, who speaks little English and almost no Hindi, feels secure in the neighbourhood. "I can't go back. I am not moving any further. I have no money. I can't work either," he says.

Waiting for third country resettlement
In the back alleys of Aslat Pur Gaon in Janakpuri, where houses stand neck to neck and several have the same number, Chin Chin and Plato, both Chin refugees from Myanmar, are awaiting their fate. The two came to Delhi after spending months in a refugee camp in Mizoram, hoping to get their cases approved for third country resettlement in countries including the United States or European nations.
But in Plato's case, it has been seven years.
Without a work permit, he has been working in the informal sector, where many such refugees are often exploited and work for hours and in horrible conditions without decent pay. Often, they survive on leftovers from the weekly vegetable markets, Plato says. "We are like beggars," he says.
"India does not give refugees the formal right to work but all refugees have access to work in the informal sector. This sector, according to recent media reports, constitutes 86 per cent of India's economy," Nayana Bose, from UNHCR's Delhi office, says.
There are more than 50,000 illegal Chin refugees from Myanmar in Mizoram, according to Chin Chin, who works for the Chin Human Rights Organisation and operates out of a small apartment in Aslat Pur Gaon. The number of these refugees has increased in the aftermath of Cyclone Nargis and the famine in Chin state, she says.
In a small dingy room with no windows, Si Pen, a Chin refugee, is keeping her fingers crossed. Her case for recognised refugee status in India has been rejected four times by the UNHCR.
Pen fears persecution in Myanmar. But without refugee status, she can't fend for herself. Her son works in the informal sector and earns Rs 1,000 a month, which is not enough for the family, she said.

Heading: Check, check, Mic Testing - Indian Express
Content:
The Lok Adalat, organised to settle matrimonial disputes by the Delhi Legal Services Authority, earned a cheering response from litigants in over 250 cases, turning up in an attempt to settle their pending rows at the district courts on Saturday. 269 cases of matrimonial dispute, ranging from custody to alimony and domestic violence had been referred to the special Lok Adalat, the first of its kind to be held in the Capital.

The Rohini court topped the list with 11 of the 32 cases referred there resolved, followed by the Tis Hazari courts, where nine cases were fully settled and over 10 of the 64 cases reported saw partial settlements.

For the litigants, the Lok Adalat was a fair bargain, as most saw it as a chance to end their never-ending rounds of the district courts. "I am relieved that my ordeal is over and I have been granted compensation. My alimony case had been pending in court for over three years now," Afshan Gul said.

Twenty-eight year old Afshan, who got married in 2000, had in 2006 moved out of her matrimonial home owing to alleged physical and mental abuse by her husband. She subsequently filed a case for maintenance against her husband.

Her case was finally resolved in the Lok Adalat at Tis Hazari Courts, and she was awarded alimony of Rs 2.5 lakh. "I am satisfied and now I just want to concentrate on the well-being of my five-year-old daughter," she said.

The idea behind the Lok Adalat was to settle disputes at the pre-litigation stage itself, considering the huge backlog of cases in courts. "This idea was mooted by Justice Ajit Prakash Shah, Chief Justice, Delhi High Court and Justice Mukul Mudgal, also of the Delhi High Court," a Delhi Legal Services Authority member said.

"The idea was unique, as besides minimising litigation and reducing its costs, the Lok Adalat also offered a platform for many parties to sit across the table and think of a compromise," advocate Dipika Jain, who was acted as a mediator, said.

"One does not expect that complex cases of matrimonial disputes can be settled in a few hours but giving them a chance to think and reach a compromise is an excellent attempt," M L Sahni, Presiding Officer at the special court constituted in Tis Hazari, said.

Buoyed by the response to its "experiment", the Delhi Legal Services Authority intends to hold similar sessions more frequently in the future. "We will request the High Court to let us hold more Lok Adalats in the future," Sanjay Sharma, Project Officer, Delhi Legal Services Authority, said.

Afraid of coming alone, people keep counsel
A vital characteristic of Lok Adalats, which makes them different from regular court proceedings, is that a litigant can do away with representation by a lawyer, for there are no legal technicalities involved. However, this characteristic was missing on Saturday, as lawyers were present in at least 90 per cent of the cases.
Most of the litigants, who had agreed to refer their cases from various courts to the Lok Adalat for settlement by way of negotiation and mediation, were flanked by their counsel, even though they were not required. Newsline asked a few litigants as to why they opted to attend the proceedings accompanied by a counsel, when they had the opportunity to simply sit across the table, talk to their spouses and settle disputes with the help of mediators presiding over the negotiation.
Sanjeev Sharma, whose matrimonial dispute has been lingering since 1996, said that since there were multiple cases lodged by his wife against him, he was apprehensive that she would come up with new allegations during the hearing. "I wanted my lawyer by my side to help me out in such a situation and present a suitable defence before the officers," Sharma said. Similarly, Mohd Kamil, whose wife filed an alimony case against him, looked upset after his lawyer failed to appear in court. "I am worried. I have never appeared in any court hearing without a lawyer. Though this is not a usual court hearing, I am still not ready to agree to a decision taken by the officers," Kamil said.
A number of litigants accepted they knew they did not need lawyers, but they just did not want to "take any chances". Officers presiding over the Lok Adalat said the issues of matrimonial dispute were different and much more complex than those settled in traffic Lok Adalats. "A number of parties approached us with multiple cases, ranging from domestic violence to alimony and sometimes even divorce. Moreover, they don't have absolute faith in the judiciary," M L Sahni, presiding officer at Tis Hazari Courts, said.

Heading: History’s bank - Indian Express
Content:
Unleash the artist in you at the Open Mic, the city's new platform to be heard and seen

Mohammed Abood aka MC Shorty looks forward to Tuesday evenings. That's when the Open Mic event gets underway at Retro Sushi, Jaypee Vasant Continental, and the Iraqi MC with a penchant for battle-rap knows he's got to be really terrific to survive on stage for even five minutes. Because the Open Mic nights are more than the city's newest platform for budding artists, here, the audience review comes instantly and usually, with brutal honesty.

"I've always wanted to perform but there aren't many venues for rappers in Delhi that let you interact with a live audience," says Abood, 21, a part of Delhi's underground hip-hop movement. He and his brotherhood no longer need to stay underground anymore, Open Mic nights are slowly changing the face of live performances in the Capital and you don't need a famous last name to be appreciated.

The idea first struck Penelope Spencer, head of events at Retro Sushi, in September. "Retro Sushi was just launching and we wanted to do out-of-the-box events of international standards," she says. Open Mic nights in the West usually include musicians and singers who perform their original scores but Spencer wanted to broaden the roster for performers here.

The nights are a rage among Delhi's hip and talented youth. "We don't have to organise a gig to be seen," says a budding guitarist.

Spencer is flooded with registrations from singers, rappers, comedians, poets and percussionists. "Most of the performances are original and the rawest form of this comes through spontaneous jams and random collaborations that happen during the evening. Sometimes, people recite poems written by their favourite poet," says Spencer, a professional singer-songwriter who occasionally joins in with her own songs.

Audience plays a significant role here. One dancer found , to her dismay, that just a pretty costume cannot curry favour with a crowd that wants to see a good show. She was booed off stage. "The best part about the event is the immediate response from the crowd. If you're good or bad or plain pathetic, you find out quickly," says Abood. He's survived several nights already, so there's still hope.

Heading: Off, on, or at back: it’s centrestage at the Week! - Indian Express
Content:
Every Diwali, people bring out their collection of coins. But for some, this is a year-long obsession

Coins that his mother gave him every Diwali initiated young IT professional Nikhil Ranjan into numismatics. "My mother is a history teacher and instead of gifting the usual Lakshmi-Ganesh coins, or temple tokens as they called, she makes it a point to buy a silver antique coin every year from an authorised jeweller. Most of these coins are those issued by British monarchs like George VI. As a child, I used to cherish these coins and that was also the beginning of my hobby," says Ranjan. Despite having a collection of nearly 1,000 coins from across the world, Ranjan considers himself an amateur collector.

For media professional Akanksha Mittal, collecting coins, stamps, picture postcards, posters have been a hobby since childhood and of these, she says, coins are something she loves to flaunt. "It started with collecting coins from across the world. Gradually, as I became interested in the history of the subcontinent, I started collecting Indian coins. From the narrow bylanes near Lal Darwaza in Ahmedabad to the Sharafa Bazaar in old Delhi to the Sunday book bazaar in Daryaganj, I have collected them from both authorised dealers and roadside vendors. A chance visit to a coin exhibition some six-seven years ago made me realise what a 'real' collection looks like," she says, adding that since then she has taken up her hobby seriously. "After all, by collecting antique coins, one is also preserving a part of one's own heritage." From the South Indian panam, the smallest coin, to punch-mark coins of ancient India to Akbar's dam—she has a range of coins.

Arvind Chandra, retired executive director of Railway Ministry, too, started as an amateur collector while he was posted at Kolkata. Today, he has more than 10,000 coins of which 200 are rare ones. "Post retirement, and in the last five years collecting coins have become a passion for me," says Chandra. And with 300 books on coins in his personal library, Chandra is a walking encyclopedia on coins. "I have travelled across the country in search of coins. At times, laborious hunts have proved to be futile and at others, I have got much more than my expectations," he says recalling a visit to the temple town of Maheshwar near Indore where he got a rare coin for his collection. Chandra specialises in Islamic coins and claims that the variety found in Indian coinage is unparallel in the entire world. "And within India, Delhi has the most number of varieties," he adds.

Perhaps that's one of the reasons why the city has one of the oldest and largest coin collectors' associations. The Delhi Coin Society, formed in 1996, has more than 300 members. Every month, the members meet at least once to discuss new findings and every year in November the Society organises a three-day exhibition of coins, banknotes and medals. Dealers, collectors, students and coin-enthusiasts from Delhi and other states participate in the show, says Chandra, the organisation's present president.

One of the oldest members of the society,

S. L. Goga Jain, is also one of the prominent dealers of antique coins in the country, having bagged a gold medal for his collection at an international show in1990. Jain, who plunged into this business in 1969 with a paltry investment of Rs 300, says "there's hardly any business as profitable and as satisfying as this one". He was initiated into numismatics as a hobby by his father, who was a collector too. "I do not sell my father's or my own collection," says Jain whose clients are both domestic and international. Asked about his most significant collection, he says with a smile: "Coins of the Sultans of Delhi."

Heading: Mock drill at Priya Cinema - Indian Express
Content:
As the fashion weeks draw to a close, divided designers & harried buyers breathe sigh of relief

Gone are the days when buyers walking back from fashion events with carts full of designer clothes was a common site, thanks to a divided Indian fashion fraternity, hosting two mega events simultaneously at two different locations this week.

Fashion Design Council of India is hosting Wills Lifestyle India Fashion Week at Pragati Maidan, and its splinter group Fashion Foundation of India is holding Delhi Fashion Week, about 15 km away, at Vasant Kunj.

If the buyers — most of them with limited budgets — want maximum variety at minimum prices, they would have to take a look of both shows after jostling through ever-so-disorderly and chaotic traffic on the Capital's roads for an hour at least, says an international buyer.

"There is no logic for organising two shows at the same time.... Buyers are hopping from one show to another and even then not able to properly study the creativity of Indian designers," Kimaya's owner Pradeep Hirani said. Echoing similar views, Dar Usha, managing director of Kuwait-based Hiba Al-Ateeqi said, "Earlier it used to be easy as Delhi had only one fashion week."

But it's difficult for buyers to "attend the shows as it takes too much time to commute from one place to another. We do not expect the fashion industry to be divided."

And the designers, too, are not happy with the split as they used to showcase their talent together; that is, before the creation of Sumit Nair-led FFI. Rohit Bal, one of the country's leading fashion designers, said: "I wish we all can come together again. That will be more productive and beneficial for the Indian fashion industry."

Fellow designer Bobby Grover said, "If divided, the fashion industry will not survive. We all need to come together again to be powerful and have better global reach."

Heading: Trader abducted from Narela market - Indian Express
Content: Delhi Police senior officers conducted a mock drill on Saturday to check the response of its own men in a terrorist attack, at Priya Complex, Vasant Vihar in the afternoon. According to the police, the drill started around 2.40 pm and lasted for about half-an-hour. After a call was flashed on the PCR, the fire brigade, a bomb squad and the special task force about a bomb being detected at Priya Complex in Vasant Vihar. The police said though the police personnel realised that it was a mock drill after reaching on the spot, they continued their efforts. Police ambulances were ready to take the injured to hospital. Special teams, bomb disposal and detection squads also swung into action.

Heading: Killing Fields - Indian Express
Content:
A 45-year-old man was allegedly abducted from Narela area of Outer district on Saturday. According to the police, they received a call about the incident around 8.20 am on Saturday while the abduction occurred around 8.15 am.

Surender Kumar, a grain merchant from Murthal, Sonepat, had come to Narela — something he did everyday. As soon as he entered the market where his shop - Surender Kumar Murthal Wale - is situated, he was allegedly dragged into a car with four to five men who escaped from the spot within seconds.

The police officers said no one could even note down the vehicle number as everything happened very quickly. Surender Kumar is a resident of Murthal and used to come to the Capital daily by train. He has been trading in Narela Mandi for the past 25 years. Police added Surender's family has not received any ransom call as yet and they are investigating the matter.

Surender's brother, meanwhile, told the police that he received a call 45 minutes after the abduction from Surender's mobile phone. Surender reportedly said he has been kidnapped by four or five men. "When Surender's brother called on the mobile phone again, it was switched off and the phone has been giving the same message ever since," a senior police officer said.

Traders of the Narela Mandi took to the roads and protested against Delhi Police alleging that security in the area is lax.

Agitators blocked the busy Narela-Bawana road and shouted anti-police slogans. The situation was brought under control only when the senior police officers reached the spot.

Police sources have also said that a team under the supervision of Assistant Commissioner of Police (Narela), Dinesh Kumar Gupta, has been formed to investigate the matter. A case of kidnapping was also registered at the Narela police station in connection with the matter on Saturday.

Police officers said they had alerted their counterparts in other states and sealed borders.

"It would be easier to track them within the Capital, hence we have sealed the necessary borders and have also flashed a message to police officers of adjoining states," a senior police officer said.

Deputy Commissioner of Police (Outer district), Atul Katiyar was not available for comment, despite repetitive attempts.

Heading: Break Point - Indian Express
Content:
This Israeli playwright hates violence. So why do all her plays deal with war?

Israeli playwright Ruth Kanner is never at a loss for creative inspiration — "one never is when one comes from a country that's always at war." Her repertoire deals with hostility and their social imprints, making this 52-year-old one of the most significant dramatists in Israel today. In Delhi for the IIC Experience, she will stage three award-winning plays—- Discovering Elijah, Amos and The Woman who Preferred to Search for Food.

"While flying to Delhi, we crossed Afghanistan and Iran and all the while I was thinking, 'what if we're forced to parachute down? They hate us because we're Jewish and we'd be shot dead," she recalls. On stage, this fear is translated into several dark stories. Amos, for instance, is a tale of a lovable field mouse that is stuck in a pipe and must make a surrealistic decision about death; it's a situation that many young soldiers in the trenches had to confront. Discovering Elijah, about the Yom Kippur War of 1973, shows how war marks its warriors even in times of peace. "These men are used to constant fighting and firing," she explains. The Woman is a grotesque account of a journey through a hunger-stricken country.

Kanner's first brush with theatre was when she was 13. "I was on a scout trip when we came across a building. I peeped through a window and saw a magical world in which actors dressed in colourful costumes were dancing in a fantastical world."

She went on to act with the Israeli Defence Army Theatre before switching to direction and winning several awards; the Landau Awards and the Rosenbaum award among them. Dead bodies and killing fields litter her productions as she pursues different perspectives. "I also love Shakespeare but I'll never do a feel-good, romantic drama," she says. Reality, she adds, will always creep into her works.

The plays will be held at the IIC on October 20. Contact: 24619431

Heading: Make-up Man - Indian Express
Content:
At the Fiama Di Wills Salon at the Wills Lifestyle India Fashion Week, the buzz was about the makeover session of south Indian actor Ileana D'Cruz on Friday. The petite actor, who was first spotted in a Fair and Lovely ad with director Rakesh Roshan a few years ago, was rumoured to have had signed a movie opposite Shahrukh Khan. But when D'Cruz finally did make her appearance after the last show of the day, she was quick to dispel the rumours. "I don't know how it started but people have been asking me about it. There's not been any talk of any movie with Shahrukh. I wish there was though," sighs the 21-year old, who is a big name in south.

With a host of successful Telugu films to her credit since her debut in YVS Chowdhary's Devadasu in 2006, D'Cruz is now looking to break in to Bollywood. But the actor asserts she is in no hurry. "Obviously, it's something that I would like to explore, but I am a firm believer in the adage that there's a right time for everything. Tollywood has been very good to me. So I'm happy with the way things have shaped up so far," she says. But when Bollwood comes calling D'Cruz has her wish list ready. "The Mumbai film industry has some really good looking actors. I would love to work with Imran Khan or Harman Baweja," she grins.

Heading: No Kidding - Indian Express
Content: In keeping with the kitschy, wildly colourful themes on his garments, designer Manish Arora, completely revamped minimalist bar, Aqua at Park Hotel, to launch his limited edition make-up collection by Mac. The backdrop at Aqua was a phallic shaped lipstick while a makeshift ramp had shocking pink, oversized palm trees on either side — except models didn't come careening down the ramp, but plonked themselves on chairs wearing striking baroque inspired make-up. Arora, visibly enjoying the party, said, "After designing cars, watches and garments of course, this was next." Will we see socialites and models flaunt these titillating and wild colours on their face? "It is baroque and it's in," smiled Arora, breezily swivelling a glass of wine. Guests sporting his Indian goddess's shirts milled around enjoying the ambience. Spotted enjoying the party were Benedict Alliot, French cultural attachee in a Manish Arora T-shirt, Caroline Young, Ambassador of France, Jerome Bonnafont, socialite Tanisha Mohan and Ameeta Seth.

Heading: A community’s cathartic call: ‘Scattered Voices’ bring forth the angst and anxiety of 2002 riot victims - Indian Express
Content:
After celebrities attempt to prove their artistic prowess, Khushii gets children to wield the brush

The annual Khushii 'India on Canvas' auction, that brings together celebrities and artists has shifted to Dubai this year but for Delhiites who are now accustomed to city celebrities brandishing a paint brush, the NGO has lined up an alternative, children. Today, the walls of the French Embassy in Delhi will be decorated with canvases made by children of celebrities, in collaboration with renowned artists. Amid the 141 canvases on display will be Raveena Tandon's three-year-old daughter Rasha's artwork painted with Gunjan Cowlagi and Kapil Dev's daughter Amiya, 12, has joined hands with Sanjay Kumar. Actor Sushmita Sen's daughter, Rene, 12, has shown her artistic prowess on a canvas with Devyani Parikh and Manpreet Brar's children, Om, 4 and Lakshmie, 2, have painted with Sidharth, Sudip Roy and Dharmendra Rathore. "The project is a result of the keen interest shown by children when artists visited celebrity homes to paint during the past auctions organised by Khushii," states Ravneet Gill, associate member, Khushii.

So while in the public domain, Lalit Kala Akademi is considering the proposition of promoting art by suspending prints of work by modern artists in classrooms in Kendriya Vidyalaya and Navodaya Schools across the country. A similar endeavour had Khushii organise three-day workshops for children. Held during the last three months, costing Rs 25,000, this had artists paint along with children on a common canvas. "The aim was to let them explore their talent without inhibitions," states artist Sidharth. The collaborated canvas with Om has a figure with folded hands painted over an abstract landscape. "The initiative helped introduce children to the nuances of art," adds Manpreet Brar.

Artist Sangeeta Murthy agrees. In her collaborative acrylic on canvas with Yuv, 13, son of businessman Sumant Bharat Ram, she has depicted her passion for architecture and his interest in sport on a blue backdrop. "We wanted it to be a work that represented our interests so that it would be a truly combined effort," says she.

The canvases that will go back to children post the exhibition are not on sale but collectors could bid for some of the works painted by children from NGOs like Balvihar and Pratham and artwork created over paw prints of elephants for a project initiated by Wildlife SOS. "The proceeds will be passed to the respective NGOs," says Gill. For Khushii, on the other hand, funds will pour in from the Dubai auction scheduled on November 29. This is where the NGO will exhibit canvases painted by David Beckham, Patricia Mills and Ratan Tata amid others. "This will be closely monitored," smiles Gill, looking forward to the Middle East sojourn. For the more humble Delhiites, meanwhile, all roads lead to the French Embassy.

Heading: Gujarat delegation finds navigation tough in Pak waters - Indian Express
Content:
The first ever anthology of intensely cathartic poems capturing the collective angst and deep anxieties of Gujarat's Muslim community that fell prey to the 2002 post-Godhra riots, was released by some of the state's leading writers at the Gujarati Sahitya Parishad here on Saturday.

The anthology, 'Scattered Voices', and its Hindi adaptation, Kuch to kaho yaaro, were edited and compiled by Ayesha Khan, assistant editor with The Indian Express, Ahmedabad.

The anthology, which took three years to put together, is an unusual collection of verses from poets who are both known and unknown, responding in their own earthy metiers and ways to the horrors of the 2002 riots and its aftermath.

Besides some of Gujarat's well-known Muslim poets, others who have been included in the collection belong to all conceivable sections of the community, including a village butcher and an autorickshaw driver, among others.

According to its publishers, Books For Change, it is an attempt to document unusual voices responding in unusual times, to unusual acts and unusual silences.

Referring to the book's raison d'etre, Ayesha Khan said the three years of labour and pains that it took to put together the book underlined its need. "The deafening silences after the 2002 riots, except for some largely ineffectual criticism by the national media, have been searching for voices that belonged to that very state, articulated in the same cultural milieu and language. It was the inadequate literary response by Gujaratis themselves, more so the Gujarati Muslims, that was more disturbing," she said.

The book, she said, was an attempt to make up for the silences that continue to numb the collective responses of a marginalised, brutalised and isolated people.

Addressing the function, noted writer and columnist Esther David recalled the frozen turbulence of the days of the 2002 riots and its implications. Others who spoke included renowned Gujarati litterateurs Abid Shamsi, Himanshi Shelat, Raghuvir Chaudhuri and Sarup Dhruv.

Heading: New technology to check fishermen from straying into Pak waters - Indian Express
Content:
Even after 12 days, members yet to meet state fishermen lodged in Pakistani jails

The seven-member delegation from Gujarat visiting Pakistan to address the issue of the release of Indian fishermen and boats might not return with any good news for the distraught families waiting back home. Though only three days are left for their 15-day tour to come to an end, the delegation has so far not been granted permission to visit the Indian fishermen lodged in Pakistani jails.

This is the first official delegation to visit Pakistan to take up the issue of Gujarati fishermen lodged in jails there. It comprises members of the Indian Fishing Forum and state Fisheries Superintendent Mahendra Chaudhary as the state government representative.

The state government decided upon sending a delegation after the Indian authorities received a communiqué from Pakistan informing them that the seized boats would be auctioned if the two sides failed to reach an amicable solution before October 30.

So far, the delegation has only inspected 142 boats seized by the Pakistani authorities, while the rest comprising nearly 60 per cent of the total number of boats seized in the last few years have been auctioned off.

According to official figures, at present, 434 fishermen and 369 boats worth over Rs 40 crore are in the custody of Pakistani authorities.

Incidentally, Pakistan has stopped the practice of releasing boats along with fishermen, since 2003.

The delegation is seemingly upset on being granted permission to inspect only 142 of the 369 Indian boats.

Bharat Modi, a member of the delegation, said: "There is just no sign of the rest of the boats. The Pakistani authorities have told us that some of those boats had already been auctioned."

Vice-President of the Indian Fishing Forum (IFF), Veljibhai Masani, told Newsline from Karachi that: "Despite repeated pleas, the Pakistani authorities have so far refused to grant us permission to meet any of the 434 fishermen and inspect certain boats in their custody."

Modi added: "The Pakistani authorities have refused us permission to meet the fishermen citing security concerns following a confrontation between some Pathan prisoners and the jail staff recently. We have been told that the jail atmosphere is not safe for visitors."

He further said: "It is becoming extremely clear that we will get back only 142 of the total 369 boats. Besides, half of these are in extremely bad shape and will require a repairing cost of at least Rs 2 -3 lakh before they are fit for sailing back to India."

Many of these fishermen have taken loans for buying the boats and their inability to repay the loan along with the deteriorating economic condition have hit hard their families settled along coastal Saurashtra and south Gujarat.

Heading: Bear hug gets deadlier: Another businessman ends life in city - Indian Express
Content:
A combo of GPS and GIS to create a virtual fencing along international border

Even as an official delegation from Gujarat is camping in Karachi to secure the early release of as many as 369 fishing boats seized by the Pakistan Maritime Security Agency, the state government has decided to introduce a vessel tracking and warning system to avert frequent incidents of fishermen straying into Pakistani waters.

The advanced technology system will be jointly implemented by the Gujarat Maritime Board (GMB) and the state Fisheries Department. The GMB will provide Rs 40 crore while the Fisheries Department will chip in with Rs 28 crore, for the project.

"We have asked the GMB to purchase the vessel tracking and warning system immediately after the current process of finalising technical specifications by the Board is over. The government plans to introduce this state-of-the art system at the earliest," said Gujarat Ports and Transport Secretary H K Dash.

He told Newsline on Saturday that the system, when introduced, will not only help check frequent incidents of Gujarati fishermen straying into Pakistani waters, but also aid in rescue operations at the time of natural calamities like cyclone, by faster communication on the high seas.

Dash said the system will function on a combination of Global Positioning System (GPS) and Geographic Information System (GIS) and create a geo-fence — a sort of virtual fencing along the International Boundary Line (IBL) between India and Pakistan.

Under the system, a data centre on the shore will monitor and control the movement of vessels using a two-way secured, non-hackable radio communication. Each of the fishing boats will have an embedded digital contraption that will get activated and alarm the fishermen the moment they cross over the border.

Under the project, the fishermen will also be provided with biometric cards, which they will have to swipe before leaving the shore and swipe again on return, with the control room registering the dates. "This will help us ascertain who all are in the sea in case of natural disaster or accident," said an official.

Deputy Secretary (Fisheries) V T Kharadi said his department has already accorded an administrative sanction to the project and contributed its share of Rs 28 crore. On its part, the GMB is busy working out all relevant technological aspects of the system. "We hope the entire vessel tracking and warning system will be in place very shortly," Kharadi added.

Heading: Lunar links: Moon mission owes a lot to Ahmedabad - Indian Express
Content:
40-year-old Jitu Parmar had invested heavily in the stock market

A 40-year-old businessman from Usmanpura allegedly committed suicide by consuming poison late on Friday.

This is the second case of suicide within 24 hours because of the recent recession in the market. On Friday morning, Meghaninagar-based financer Jitu Parmar allegedly hanged himself in his residence near Jethalal Park because of the losses due to the market downslide.

The police said Dinesh Shah had invested heavily into shares and the recent slump in the market was the probable reason behind him taking the extreme step. "His family members have told us that Shah was disturbed because of the slump. At this point of time, market recession seems to be the reason that provoked Shah to take the extreme step," the police said.

The police added that Shah, who owned a chemical factory in the city, was dizzy when he came to his house at the Gujarat Middle Class Society near Shantinagar in Usmanpura around 8 pm on Friday. His family members rushed him to a private hospital, when the latter started vomiting. Doctors on duty declared Shah dead around 11.30 pm, the police said.

The Naranpura police have registered a case of accidental death and are awaiting Shah's postmortem report.

Meanwhile, the Meghaninagar police, which is investigating the Parmar suicide case, said on Saturday that they are trying to ascertain the actual amount of money that Parmar had lost because of the market slump.

"His wife Neeta, who probably knows about Parmar's investments, is still in a state of shock and we are yet to record her statement," said Inspector S F Saiyed.

Heading: Another Gujarat bank now has Maharashtra ownership - Indian Express
Content:
Many critical components of Chandrayaan-1 were developed at city's ISRO centre

When PSLV-C11 blasts off on October 22 from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh with Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar mission, on board will be the dreams and efforts of a clutch of scientists from Ahmedabad's Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

Several highly critical components for the mission were developed at ISRO, Ahmedabad.

The mission will last about two years and aim to unravel the mysteries of the moon, which still remains much of an enigma for the scientific community.

Questions relating to the origin and evolution of the moon, the presence of water, the mineralogical composition and the quantification of helium-3 (a clean fuel for the future nuclear fusion reactors) still pose a puzzle to the scientists, and ISRO envisages finding answers to these questions. For this, Chandrayaan-1 will use its high resolution remote sensing sensors to view the moon in the visible, near infrared, microwave and X-ray regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Chandrayaan-1 will carry 11 payloads (scientific instruments). Of these, five are India's very own, three are from the European Space Agency (ESA), two are from NASA and one is from Bulgaria.

The Indian payloads include the Terrain Mapping Camera, Hyperspectral Imager, High Energy X-ray Spectrometer, Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument (LLRI) and a 29 kg Moon Impact Probe (MIP).

While the LLRI will provide the necessary data for determining the accurate altitude of Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft above the lunar surface, the MIP will pave way for future soft landing missions on the moon by demonstrating the technologies required for landing a probe at the desired location.

Among the equipment developed at Ahmedabad is the Terrain Mapping Camera (TMC). This will completely map the topography of the moon with a resolution of 5 metres. It can image a strip of the lunar surface about 20 km wide and will work in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum, capturing black and white stereo images. The data from the TMC along with the one collected by the Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument will help scientists map the lunar gravitational field as well.

Another is the Hyperspectral Imager (HySI), also built by ISRO's Space Application Centre, Ahmedabad. This will help map minerals on the lunar surface along with the mineralogical composition of the moon's interior. This imager, with a resolution of 80 metres and operating in the visible and near infrared regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, can image a strip about 20 km wide.

The High Energy X-ray Spectrometer (HEX), jointly built by the Physical Research Laboratory, Ahmedabad and ISRO's Satellite Centre at Bangalore is another key equipment, which will identify polar regions covered by thick water-ice deposits. It will also identify regions of high uranium and thorium concentrations on the moon. Incidentally, this is the first planetary experiment relating to spectral studies of X-ray energies, and is hoped to throw light on the evolution and origin of the moon.

The spacecraft, which will weigh about 1,400 kg at launch and about 590 kg in the lunar orbit, is cuboid in shape with a solar panel generating a maximum of 700 watts, projecting from one of its sides. Alternately, it also has a 36 Ampere-Hour (Ah) lithium-ion battery. To attain the escape velocity and travel towards moon, the spacecraft has a Liquid Apogee Motor (LAM).

The 44.4 m tall launch vehicle also has strap-on motors (PSOM-XL) for achieving higher payload capabilities. The vehicle will use solid and liquid propulsion systems alternately in four stages.

It will begin its journey by reaching a highly elliptical initial orbit (IO) with a perigee (nearest point to earth) of 250 km and an apogee (farthest) of 23,000 km. After circling the earth in its IO for a while, the LAM will fire to lift the spacecraft to an orbit of apogee 3,87,000 km. In this orbit, the spacecraft will make one complete revolution around the earth in about 11 days. Subsequently, the orbit will finally be lowered to the intended 100 km height from the lunar surface. Later on, the MIP will be ejected from the spacecraft to hit the lunar surface, beginning the operational phase of the mission, which will last two years.

Heading: Police suspect doctors’ hand behind abandoned foetuses - Indian Express
Content:
Mumbai's Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank takes over Manekchowk Co-operative Bank

Maharashtra has bagged yet another co-operative bank from Gujarat in its kitty. The Mumbai-based Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank (ACB) has acquired the Manekchowk Co-operative Bank. Earlier, the Pune-based Cosmos Bank had acquired the Co-operative Bank of Ahmedabad.

The much-awaited RBI nod for the merger was given on October 16, when the Central bank cancelled banking licence of the Manekchowk Bank and granted branch licence to the ACB. The Manekchowk Bank was in news for quite some time and its liquidation was on the cards when the ACB made the bid to bag the jewellers' bank.

While Manekchowk chairman Girish Choksi was not available for comment, sources in the bank said that its liabilities are being worked out at present. None of the 100-odd staff will be laid off even as fresh ACB nominees have replaced the entire board of directors of the Manekchowk Bank, they said.

The merger has cost the ACB Rs 22 crore. The Manekchowk Bank has a capital base of Rs 30 crore, deposits Rs 23 crore and advances, Rs 17 crore. On the other hand, the ACB, which was established in 1964 with a deposit base of Rs 5,000 and 83 members, now has a deposit base of Rs 2,600 crore, which grew by Rs 500 crore from the previous year.

The ACB had acquired the Shrikrishna Bank in Vadodara in June and the Janta Sahakari Bank, Udupi in August this year. It now has over 1.10 lakh members. With the acquisition, ACB will now have 71 branches across the country.

Heading: Economic slump affects outbound tourist traffic during festive season - Indian Express
Content:
A day after four foetuses were recovered from plastic bags lying in a dry canal in Rasana village of Deesa taluka the police suspect the involvement of medical practitioners and nearby hospitals in the racket.

Banaskantha Superintendent of Police D N Patel hasn't ruled out the possibility of a racket. He said: "Preliminary investigations point towards the involvement of doctors or some hospital. The involvement of villagers isn't a possibility given the manner in which the foetuses were disposed. As to why the foetuses were disposed will only be determined after we get the report, which will confirm whether the termination of pregnancy was legal under the MTP (Medical Termination of Pregnancy) Act or not. But as of now, we suspect a clear involvement of medical practitioners. It can also be a case of female foeticide."

The foetuses have been sent for postmortem to the Civil Hospital in Deesa and the police are awaiting the report. Along with other factors, the report will determine the sex and age of the foetuses.

While the sarpanch of Rasana village spotted the plastic bags on Thursday, the Deesa Taluka police station registered a complaint on Friday. Investigating Officer, Inspector U R Thakore said: "The nearest village from the canal where the foetuses were found is at least 2 kilometres away. The area happens to be a remote one and is hardly frequented by villagers. Moreover, since the spot is close to NH-5 and the bags were found in a dry canal under a connecting bridge, it is possible that someone must have thrown the bags and fled."

Heading: In a first, 60 disabled students secure admission in MBA courses run by self-financed colleges - Indian Express
Content:
As A ripple effect of the global recession and the resultant economic slump, the usual upswing in the outbound traveller traffic to various getaway destinations before Diwali seems to be missing this year.

Travel agents estimate the loss in business to the tune of 30 to 35 per cent in Ahmedabad alone, while in cities like Vadodara and Surat, the business has gone down by 50 per cent as compared to the previous season. In Rajkot, a 40 to 45 per cent dip has been witnessed in the outbound holiday traffic.

Tour organisers in the state believe that a sizeable number of travellers have cancelled their holiday plans due to rising airfares and travel expenses. "International trips have gone down due to increased airfares," said a travel agent from Club 7 Holidays.

The airlines have also witnessed a sizeable dip in reservations as compared to last year.

Airport Manager Sachin Bohalekar said: "The usual upswing in business during Diwali after the off-season period hasn't been seen this year. The overall number of travellers has gone down by 20 to 25 percent. The US bound traffic has been affected in a major way, but the UK bound traffic hasn't been affected much. With the markets crashing in the last 15-20 days, the domestic travellers have also been hit badly. Compared to last years' airfares, this year every airline has increased its tariff."

Tour to foreign destinations has also seen a substantial decrease in Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara and Rajkot. A travel agent in Ahmedabad said: "Destinations like Kerala, Kanyakumari, Ooty, Darjeeling, Shimla and Jammu and Kashmir are the ones which have been affected the most. Mount Abu, Daman, Mahabaleshwar and Goa remain to be in demand, though."

An agent from Shells Travel Service in the city said: "In Ahmedabad, business is lower by 20 to 25 percent this year. Instead of Australia and New Zealand, travellers have shown a preference for Italy and Egypt."

In Vadodara, the tourism industry has come to a temporary stop. "The business is totally down. Kerala and Kanyakumari costs the same as Singapore which is why people are heading to these destinations," said an agent from United International Tours in Vadodara.

Thomas Cook is also experiencing a falling trend in Surat because of the recession and the Income Tax raids.

"A family had booked tickets for December, but then had them cancelled because of the Income Tax raid," said an agent from Thomas Cook.

Jayendrasinh Zala from Transline Tours in Vadodara, however, said that despite the recession, he is getting many inbound and outbound bookings, as Gujaratis are holiday lovers by nature.

"The increasing use of travel portals has reduced the number of people booking at travel and tour agencies. We offer tailor-made tours to the customers and my business is doing well in this season also," he said.

He added that this year Sikkim and Darjeeling are the most preferred places, followed by Rajasthan and Kerala. There are discounted and attractive packages available to the customers, he added.

According to Tourism Corporation of Gujarat officials, the nature of tourism has changed in the state this year and Gujarat is expecting a good percentage of outsiders this Diwali like every year. Gujarat has always been famous for religious tourism and will witness a steady growth of corporate and business tourism this year, they said.

- With inputs from Amrita Didyala and Ujjwala Nayudu

Heading: Lecture theatres at six medical colleges to become ‘smart’ - Indian Express
Content:
Even as Articles 32 and 39 of the PWD (Persons With Disability) Act, 1995 clearly pronounces that every academic institution is bound to reserve 3 per cent of the seats for the disabled students, this seems to have been ignored by most of the self-financed institutions in the state.

This academic year though, a total of 60 disabled students (Ortho-handicapped and low vision) have secured admission in an MBA course in self financed colleges in the state, following the policy implementation under the two Articles of the Act.

R M Patel, in-charge, Disability Commissioner said: "Although the 3 per cent reservation rule has been there right from 1995, like other quotas, it has not been implemented properly all this time. A total of 100 seats have been reserved for the disabled students."

But only 60 of the seats have been filled under this category as most students refrain from enrolling in colleges, he said. The figure is, nevertheless, a staggering increase from the usual 5-6 each year, he added.

Former Disability Commissioner Bhaskar Mehta said: "Polytechnic, dental and medical seats under the reservation quota for disabled students generally don't have any takers. But this has been for the first time that 60 students have secured admissions in self-financed colleges."

According to Mehta, one of the major reasons why most of the seats have remained vacant is probably the prejudice towards disabled students, which prevents them from enrolling, besides the students' low-self confidence.

"The self-financed colleges largely had an unaccommodating attitude. In fact, the low vision disability wasn't even differentiated from visually impaired whereas the two are completely different." he said.

Incidentally, Mehta had initiated the implementation of the policy by writing

repeated letters to the Education Department for the proper implementation of the Article.

While the policy has been implemented in the academic year 2008-2009; the increase in the number of disabled children enrolling in MBA courses, which the state has witnessed for the first time, has come as a breather.

Heading: Indian Coast Guard unearths liquor smuggling racket - Indian Express
Content:
To make the students conversant with e-learning systems, the lecture theatres of six government medical colleges of the state will now be equipped with LCD projectors, laptops, interactive board, interactive pads and air conditioners. The echo-proof room will be converted into 'smart lecture theatres' to facilitate a better learning process for the students.

A provision for grants for the upgradation of these theatres was decided upon at a meeting called by the director of health services, recently.

A grant of Rs 10 lakh has been given to the Baroda Medical College for the same. Dean A T Lehua said, "At least one classroom each will have to be developed as per the set format in all the six colleges."

An investment of around Rs 25 lakh is needed for the same, he added.

At present, the classrooms do not have air conditioning. Moreover, the professors use their personal laptops to give lectures and there are no interactive pads or boards as well, he added.

The grants to equip them differ from college to college, depending on the strength of the college and the level of upgradation required.

The Director of Medical Education, Dr Vitlani said, "The completion of the process will depend on the quantum of the work required. The colleges will soon chart out plans to implement it."

Heading: Sessions Court upholds lower court’s order in domestic violence case - Indian Express
Content:
The Indian Coast Guard unearthed a liquor smuggling racked through the sea route after it caught 12 fishing boats some 20 miles off the Jakhau coast on Saturday. The boats and the arrested fishermen have now been handed over to the Kutch district police for joint interrogation by various agencies including the customs and the Intelligence.

Coast Guard Commandant K L Arun said: "Indian Made Foreign Liquor was smuggled under the guise of fishing. Each boat was ferrying about 300 to 400 bottles."

The Jakhau police have now begun procedures to register a case of prohibition and smuggling against the fishermen.

Jakhau Sub-Inspector K B Parmar said: "So far, we have inspected only one boat and found around 300 bottles of IMFL."

The Coast Guard suspects the consignment could have arrived from the nearby Union Territories of Diu or Daman as the demand for liquor is likely to go up in the state during the festive season.

Heading: Government websites an easy hunt for hackers - Indian Express
Content:
The Ahmedabad District Civil and Sessions Court has in a case of domestic violence upheld an interim order of a lower court that had granted rights of residence and maintenance to the victim.

The Sessions Court also affirmed the order of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Dholka – where the case was first heard – that the victim and her two children be given maintenance amount of Rs 9,000 per month. The court has also upheld the Judicial Magistrate's order that the victim and her children, who are suffering from Wilson's disease, be paid Rs 50,000 as medical expenditure. Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder in which copper accumulates in muscle tissues.

The court further upheld the decision that the ground floor of the residential property where the victim's husband and in-laws reside be vacated for her till a further order is passed. However, the Sessions Court modified the order of the lower court slightly and said the right of residence does not apply against women and therefore the women of the family can live with the victim. The court also upheld the decision of the judicial magistrate wherein it has barred the accused from transferring property help in his name during the pendency of the trial.

The victim, who has been married for 12 years, had filed the case under the Protection of Domestic Violence Act, 2005 against her husband and in-laws. The woman claimed that her husband, a businessman in Dholka, had been mentally harassing her.

Heading: Unidentified body recovered from Vastrapur bungalow’s servant quarter - Indian Express
Content:
Server technologies of these websites are not updated, say experts

With the gen-next wave of terror fast pervading the cyber space, ethical hackers are raising concern about most government websites being vulnerable to hacking.

According to city-based ethical hacker Sunny Vaghela, over 20 websites of the Gujarat government are vulnerable to hacking. "One can easily enter these websites, access the protected information and alter them without even leaving behind any trace," he said.

While he refused to reveal the names of websites, which run such risks, he pointed out that with the developer of most such sites being common, the flaws in all of them were identical.

"One of the biggest reasons of such vulnerability is that the server technologies and the website databases are not upgraded periodically," Vaghela said. According to him, a professional hacker takes about 24 hours to hack into the sites that have such vulnerability.

To begin with, he said, one starts off with gathering information about the server administration, "They look for web applications, operating system, data base versions and the number of open ports in the targeted website," he said, adding that once the vulnerabilities of the site is identified, the hacker moves into the sites after scanning the open ports.

"Another problem with the websites of the state government is that many of them don't even maintain a web-log. This means that if somebody hacks into a site and accesses the protected information, and leaves without making any change, one will never be able to know that," he added.

Vaghela, who has been assisting the Ahmedabad Crime Branch in tracing a number of e-mails, including the one sent by the Indian Mujaheedin before the July 26 serial blasts, said he has already reported the matter to the government authorities.

Vaghela had earlier created ripples in 2006 by demonstrating how calls can be forged from mobile phones, whereby the receiver of a call will see a different caller's number on his cellphone when de-facto the call is being made by someone else.

Subhash, another ethical hacker from Hyderabad, confirmed Vaghela's claims and said that not only the government websites, but also most of the commercial portals are vulnerable. Speaking to Newsline, Gujarat Secretary Science and Technology Rajkumar said the department will soon get the security audit done through one of the empanelled organisations called Cert In.

Heading: Ahmedabad continues to grapple with mosquito-borne diseases - Indian Express
Content:
An unidentified youth was found murdered inside the servant's quarter of a bungalow in Vastrapur area on Saturday morning. The prime suspect in the case is the 30-year-old domestic help of the house, Prakash, who is presently at large.

The alleged murder took place inside the servant's quarter of no. 11 Sarthi Bungalows in Vastrapur, late on Friday. The bungalow belongs to city-based chemical businessman Ramabhai Thakkar.

The Thakkars spotted the yet-to-be-identified body in Prakash's room around 8 am on Saturday, when he did not report for his morning duties. "On opening the room's door, the Thakkars were shocked to see a body lying inside the room. The victim, aged around 25 had been strangled to death," said Vastrapur police inspector R B Joshi.

Preliminary investigations revealed that the Thakkars had last seen Prakash on Friday night. "Prakash, who is presently at large, is the prime suspect in the case," Joshi added.

Police said that Prakash hails from Rajasthan and was working as a domestic help for the Thakkars for the last two years. "Right now, our first priority is to establish the victim's identity. The other facts will follow after that," said Joshi.

Meanwhile the victim's body has been sent for a post mortem and the police are awaiting the report to ascertain the actual cause of death. The police have also roped in experts from the Directorate of Forensic Sciences (DFS) in Gandhinagar to help them in the probe.

Heading: Mob torches vehicles after truck kills boy in Tandalja - Indian Express
Content:
The city residents continue to grapple with mosquito-borne diseases as 24 fresh cases of suspected dengue have come to the notice of the civic authorities this month. Health department officials of the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) said the number is less than the cases reported in September, when it was 40.

Taking no chances, doctors took blood samples of even those patients who had come with complaints of mild fever at 19 surveillance centres, Dr S P Kulkarni, AMC medical officer said on Saturday.

According to him, 900 blood samples have been tested so far this year. One person has reportedly died of dengue, he said.

Asked if more cases were reported from the new west zone areas, Dr Kulkarni said there was not much difference between the number of cases reported from old limits and new areas. Generally, most cases are reported in the post-monsoon period, he said, adding that not all reported cases are admitted as indoor patients.

He admitted that cases of falciparum malaria were more than dengue. In October alone 71 cases of falciparum malaria were reported at civic hospitals, he said. The number has been static since July.

"The number of malaria cases should decline from November onwards," he said. It may be recalled that dengue had wrecked havoc in the city three years ago.

Heading: Priceless manuscripts fall prey to careless upkeep - Indian Express
Content:
The residents of Tandalja resorted to arson and stone pelting at vehicles after a truck crushed an eight-year-old boy to death on Saturday evening.

The Juna Padra Road police said the victim, Mohammed Shad, was a student of Experimental School. He was the only boy in the four-member family.

"Mohammed had a tuition class in the evening and soon after he came out of his house located on the Tandalja Road, near JP Road police station, a truck coming from behind ran over him," said Zohaib Shaikh, a relative of the deceased.

"There were some people who saw the accident. They got furious and indulged into stone pelting and arson," said Shaikh, who was present at the police station for lodging a complaint against the truck driver who escaped from the scene after the accident.

Officials at the J P Road police station said that while the truck, which crushed the boy, was damaged, the locals torched another truck and a Maruti 800, which were passing from the same road.

"There was a heavy stone pelting incident which continued for almost an hour. Even the fire brigade officials were not able to reach the spot early. The flames were doused around 7 pm," said a police official, adding that the situation was under control.

The irate residents even surrounded the JP Road police station, demanding strict action against the driver who was apparently driving the rashly.

Heading: MSU, ministry join hands to identify loopholes in implementation of social justice - Indian Express
Content:
MSU's Oriental Institute facing shortage of space, manpower

Despite having a priceless collection of 30,215 rare manuscripts, the Oriental Institute of Maharaja Sayajirao University (MSU) today cries for proper infrastructure for their upkeep.

This premier institute though has a reason to take pride in its rare manuscripts and ancient astronomical instruments, with some of them being collected by none other than Sayajirao Gaekwad, At present, it is woefully short of space and manpower.

Much to the embarrassment, the university authorities are not even aware that Sayajirao had donated two fireproof wooden almirah's to the Oriental Institute. It was first installed in 1927, and they are now lying unoccupied in Hansa Mehta Library.

"The almirahs were especially brought by Sayajirao Gaekwad from London to keep royal jewels. However, realising the importance of the manuscripts, the almirahs were donated to the Institute," said M L Wadekar, in-charge director of the Institute.

He added that the university engineer had said that due to its weight and 'technical reasons' they could not be shifted to the University Press where the Institute is located.

Interestingly, MSU engineer N K Oza said he is not aware of any such issue. "…Neither do I know about the problem of space faced by the Oriental Institute in keeping the manuscripts," he added.

An official of the Oriental Institute said on condition of anonymity: "There is no proper staff to maintain the manuscripts. Technically, the manuscripts should be kept in clinical laboratories. However, no attention has been paid so far."

Reacting to this, Wadekar said: "Sayajirao had a vision to build this institute much before the MSU came into existence. It was shifted to the Hansa Mehta Library so that the students could refer it. One would suggest that minimal requirement such as Internet connections, its location within the university campus as well as the space to keep the manuscripts should increase."

Jyoti Bhatt, in-charge librarian of Hansa Mehta Library, said: "The Oriental Institute was positioned at the library's ground floor from year 1949 to 1995. However, the almirahs could not be shifted. The keys are still lying with the Institute authorities and the cupboards are in the library."

Heading: At PCA, fans galore to see the Royal Bengal Tiger roar - Indian Express
Content:
For the first time, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment will work with a university to bring about changes in the implementation of social justice.

M S University's Faculty of Social Work (FSW) is conducting a two-day seminar with the Ministry titled

'Effective Implementation of Atrocity Act'. The seminar is focusing on identifying the loopholes in the system of social justice.

With paper presentations by police officers, NGOs and government officials, the ministry will incorporate the findings of the seminar in the implementation process.

On the first day, the seminar was attended by Minister of Social Justice Fakhir Vaghela and former Bombay High Court judge V H Bhairaviya.

Vaghela said: "There are many loopholes in the system. While many are not aware of the system, we have noticed that the police officers, who register FIRs, do not take much care in giving detailed information, because of which most cases do not get justice."

Statistical details also show that there were 1,124 registered cases of atrocity on the Scheduled Castes in 2007 and 972 cases have already been registered till August this year.

"The major issue here is to change the perception and mindset of the people towards every section of the society irrespective of the class. It is because of this mindset that Dalits face such problems and are still far from getting justice," said Aruna Khasgiwala, Dean, FSW.

Under the 11th Five-Year Plan, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has given the faculty five years to take up more research, developmental activities and workshops for the Dalits at Dr Ambedkar Study Centre to bring in more awareness on the issue.

Heading: Cutting congestion: No two ways about it - Indian Express
Content:
When the "Royal Bengal Tiger" roared his way to his 16th Test century on Saturday, the 10,000 odd spectators, gathered at the PCA Stadium, erupted in elation. Every run from Sourav Ganguly's blade resonated with the loud cheers of his fans as he crafted his second century against Australia.

"We were eager to see Ganguly score a century at this ground and that came, but, in his last series. We still can't believe he is retiring and we hope, he reconsiders his decision," said Pranjal Thakur, a bank executive.

The anticipation of the people could be gauged from the fact that the sparsely filled stadium in the morning session was packed by noon, as Ganguly inched closer to his ton. "Since this is his last series, we wanted to see him bat and he batted like God today. We hope he will shine with the ball too in Australia's first innings," said Sugandha Mishra, a college student.

"During the JP Atray Tournament also, Sourav was too eager to perform and I am sure he will make a big score in the second innings too," said Sushil Kapoor, one of the organisers of the JP Atray Tournament

With Australia looking down the barrel at 102 for 4 at the end of the second day's play, the chances of India batting again on Sunday is strong and this, the PCA officials hope, will bring the much-needed crowd support in the match.

Crowd awaits 'Turbanator's' 300th scalp

After seeing Tendulkar and Ganguly reach their personal milestones, the crowd is now anticipating Harbhajan Singh to get some quick wickets to take his tally beyond the 300 mark. The fans could be seen cheering for Harbhajan Singh when he was pressed into service with the "red cherry" in his hand against Australia's today.

Heading: PGI docs call off strike, to resume work today - Indian Express
Content:
Third route from Chandigarh to Panchkula set to become operational by year-end

Come December and there will be three routes connecting Chandigarh and Panchkula. Besides the existing routes - Madhya Marg leading to Housing Board lightpoint and St Kabir School Housing Board lightpoint via Information Technology Park lightpoint and Modern Housing Complex; the much-awaited route from Hallomajra village lightpoint at the Chandigarh-Zirakpur highway and connecting Panchkula's Bell factory, Industrial Area will see the light of day by mid-November.

The new path, which is about 2.9 kilometers, is under construction and will comprise a four-lane road with a median.

While talking to the Chandigarh Newsline, the UT Administration's engineers said, "The route is almost complete, except for the construction of a 100-yard bridge, which will get ready by mid-November. Another 500 metres stretch connecting the bridge to the main road will also be completed soon. There is a railway junction in between and the proposal is to construct an underpass below the railway line. If the proposal gets a green signal, commuters will save a lot of time."

Around 1.5 to 2 lakh people commute between Chandigarh and Panchkula everyday. With the Madhya Marg route and St Kabir School route already clogged, the new route will share the burden of around 40,000 vehicles.

"After the completion of the new route, the choking detours can breathe," said Sanjay Jain, Assistant Engineer, UT Administration's Engineering Department, who is supervising the construction work at the new route.

The new route will connect the roads between the Chandigarh Airport and the Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park via the railway station. It will further make the distance between Mohali and Panchkula much shorter.

Another route that connects the City Beautiful with Panchkula passes through the Saketri-Kishangarh village road. It starts from the Chandigarh Airport rotary and reaches Panchkula at various points (Industrial Area, Sector 16 and 17 through Mauli Jagran village and Rajiv Colony) crossing through Makhanmajra.

The new route will also be used to ferry goods from railway station and godowns in Daria village. Previously, trucks used to clog the Purv Marg to reach the Chandigarh Railway Station and Daria village.

The new route will

* Shorten the distance between southern sectors of Chandigarh and Mohali with Panchkula

* Bring Panchkula Industrial Area and Chandigarh Industrial Area closer

* Shorten the route connecting the airport, railway station and IT park

* Reduce congestion of vehicles at over-clogged Madhya Marg and Purv Marg

Heading: Greenpeace creates awareness about industrial pollution, climate change - Indian Express
Content:
The senior residents at the PGI called off their strike after observing one-day mass casual leave following a controversy in which the Urology department's assistant professor allegedly slapped and shouted at a senior resident.

A single day of the absence of as many as 800 resident doctors severely paralysed the normal OPD functioning at the institute. All the scheduled surgeries were cancelled as most of the rooms of the senior residents remained locked in the OPD block. The senior faculty too attended far lesser number of patients than the usual days. It was only the emergency and the ICU services that were not affected during the day.

After the late evening meeting of the Association of Resident Doctors (ARD), Dr Prabhu Shanker, president of the association, said, "In the larger interest of patients, we have decided to abort the strike and resume work from Sunday. The director has promised us that the matter will be taken up at the level of the health minister."

Despite a written apology by the consultant, the residents want the matter to be taken to the Health Minister for a disciplinary action. They are also seeking a public apology from him.

The incident occurred when Dr Sanand Kumar, senior resident, Urology, was allegedly assaulted and abused by Dr Santosh Kumar, assistant professor of the same department, in front of the hospital staff.
