"A pan-IIM Board just doesn't make sense when each institute has its own board. In fact, the older IIMs have a case for autonomy and have proven their credentials. They have a right to be freed of government control. To suggest that the HRD Ministry should decide the constitution of the IIM Board of Governors is shocking. We had earlier expressed our inability in helping the new IIMs (as suggested in the report) because of our limited faculty and resources. We had instead asked the Ministry to allow us to set up branches which they didn't," said an IIM director on condition of anonymity.

Though the report is said to have largely steered clear of the issue of fee hike, it has touched on the subject of revenue generation. The committee report is likely to ask that IIMs should go slow on income generating activities like consultancies and executive training programmes. The recommendation, if accepted and implemented by the Government, will spell bad news for the IIMs as this additional income is what helps draw and retain quality faculty to the premier institutes. The committee is also learnt to have suggested that IIMs operating for five years or more should only be making a 'small operating surplus' to be used towards infrastructure building and strengthening of scholarship funds. The Review Committee is also said to have suggested that the annual intake in Post Graduate Programmes be increased to 750.

A more welcome recommendation of the committee, based on western models, is to separate academic and administrative functions of IIMs to enable faculty to devote more time to research and teaching.

What the panel says

• A 15-member pan-IIM Board with five government nominees and chairman nominated by the PM

• Re-constitution of the Board of Governors (BoG), downsizing it from current 24-25 members to 11 

• A committee headed by Secretary, HRD Ministry, and with three independent professionals to make initial selections of BoGs

• Faculty shortage to be met with appointments on contract basis, increased output of PhDs

• All IIMs to generate only a small operating surplus. Fee for courses to be fixed keeping in mind small surplus and other incomes

• Increase annual PGP intake to 750

• IIMs to use corpus raised over base level of Rs 50 crore without any government approval/control

Heading: On day of Kabul embassy bombing, a chatter about ‘mazedaar attack’ - Indian Express
Content:
Mohammed Sadiq Sheikh, the alleged co-founder of the Indian Mujahideen, is said to have disclosed to his interrogators that Atif Ameen—who was killed in the September 19 Jamia Nagar police encounter—trained at a Lashkar-e-Toiba camp near Muzaffarabad and was in touch with Pakistan-based terrorist Amir Raza Khan.

The Mumbai Police had arrested Sadiq along with four others on September 25.

Top police officials told The Sunday Express that programme engineer Sadiq Sheikh's claim—that Atif went to Pakistan in 2002-2003 for indoctrination and for training at the Lashkar-run Bait-ul Mujahideen camp in Pakistan occupied Kashmir (PoK)—is being verified by anti-terror squads of Mumbai, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh. The UP ATS questioned the IM co-founder on his role in the November 2007 court blasts.

According to Sadiq, who is alleged to be the head of the Azamgarh module of the IM, Atif was the executor of the recent terror attacks in the country and was the liaison between IM recruiter Riyaz Bhatkal and Pakistan-based Amir Raza Khan. He said Raza contacted Atif as early as 2003 after which the group, that identified itself as IM after the UP court blasts, started planning terror attacks in India.

Security agencies and police are trying to corroborate Sadiq's claims. Police say it's extremely tedious to piece the jigsaw puzzle surrounding the terror attacks as the IM module and their Pakistan-based backers operated on a need-to-know basis.

Heading: People say I am soft on terror. What should I do? Go on shouting about it? - Indian Express
Content:
Five to six weeks before the Indian Embassy attack in Kabul on July 7, an Afghan named Mohammed Hashim walked up to the office of the Deputy Chief of Religious Police claiming that he had been approached to assist in carrying out a bomb attack on the embassy.

Hashim named an engineer, Gaffar, in Panjsher as the main collaborator who was in touch with Pakistani authorities. He claimed that Gaffar had told him that his handlers wanted a plan in a few weeks.

Hashim apparently was then asked by the police to play the role of a paid informant and was sent back. However, his phone went unreachable days before the bombing. But soon after the attack, the authorities were able to trace Hashim who claimed that he had nothing to do with the attack.

But Hashim did reveal that he had travelled to Pakistan to sell a plan and was promised remuneration for his efforts. There, according to information made available to Indian authorities, Hashim was taken to Taliban's former Deputy Foreign Minister Abdul Rehman Zahed who lives in Hayatabad, a suburb near Peshawar.

In the conversation that transpired, which Hashim narrated to Afghan authorities, Zahed explained to him that his residence in Pakistan was not without a price and so India was a "legitimate target."

Security agencies have since figured out that Zahed has a Pakistan passport on which he has even travelled to Dubai, said sources. Zahed is said to be receiving ISI patronage and was tasked with carrying out a spectacular attack against Indian assets in Afghanistan. He also has links with the Haqqani group, which US agencies first indicated had a possible role to play in the July 7 attack.

Later, at the instance of investigating agencies, Hashim made a call to his contact and demanded money for carrying out the attack. His contact said the attack had been carried out by another group. When Hashim insisted that he did it, he was given a Pakistan phone number and told to make any claims of remuneration there. The same story was repeated and the person who picked up the phone seemed to indicate that the bomber was from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

In preparing its case against Pakistan on the Kabul embassy attack, India believes it has now a convincing dossier including the trail that leads to Zahed.

Also, US agencies have shared intercepts picked up by their signal units of the conversation happening on the Pakistan side of the Pak-Afghan border on the day of the bombing in which the blast is being described as a "mazedaar attack".

India's case is bolstered by the fact that these intercepts were picked up not just by the US, but also French and Afghan agencies which have now been passed on to India.

On the investigations front, three Afghans are in custody now but their role was limited to obtaining the car and, sources said, they had no idea of the larger plan.

Only the driver who delivered the car recalls the person who received it making a long distance call, possibly to Pakistan, and informing "kaam ho gaya (the job is done)."

Another input that the Indian agencies have received is that two Pakistani intelligence officials and nine others were involved in the planning and execution of the attack.

The fact that many elements in the case are verifiable by agencies from other countries has also bolstered India's attempt to extract some meaningful response from Islamabad at the upcoming meeting of the Indo-Pak anti-terror mechanism expected to meet in a week or so.

Heading: MAGIC REALISM - Indian Express
Content:
•Shekhar Gupta: Would you comment on the current security situation, including the communal violence and the government's record on governance?

Those who are in the government would say they have done well; those outside the government would take an independent viewwhich is likely to be more correctwhile the opposition will criticise everything that the government is doing. It was a very difficult task for the government to carry all the allies and continue to perform its duties. However, due to the mature approach of all the parties, the Prime Minister and other members of the government, there have been no difficulties in governance in the area of development. This government has taken a more liberal attitude towards economic development than the previous government. This attitude has helped to attract more investments and bring about impressive economic progress. Problems have now arisen because of the global meltdown but due to the government's approach, it should be possible to protect our interests.

Agriculture is doing well. We have paid a lot of attention to making food grains easily available and to restrict imports. Employment is being generated by the NREG scheme (National Rural Employment Guarantee scheme). On the social front, we are facing a very complex situation: there are tensions developing between people of different communities. Some people who are religious and fundamentalist in attitude and have parochial feelings are creating problems.

Fortunately, there have been no threats posed to national security. Internal security has been threatened and it will be discussed in the next general elections. Such a debate is welcome to remove whatever current defects exist in the system. So far, we have paid more attention to development than to security. If there is enough security, development becomes easier. I believe we have not been able to inform the citizens properly on issues of security. National security is the responsibility of the Centre. Terrorism and crime are to be managed by the states. However, it is not possible for the Union government to say it is not responsible in any way for the current security scenario and it is wrong for the states to say we cannot cope with the situation. Cooperation between state governments and the Central government is required for the desired results. Fortunately, such coordination has been possible among all political parties.

•Ravish Tiwari: You have been in politics for very long and a Speaker of the Lok Sabha, but after losing in the 2004 general elections, did you anticipate you would be given such a big responsibility?

I have been in government for a long time. I have contested 11 elections and lost one. There is no doubt that my current job is of great importance but I have never felt burdened by it. I am not very apt in dealing with the media and that is why I think I get the flak. But I have dealt with Parliament and I know how to deal with people and the problems of the country and that is why I have not faced problems as Home Minister.

•Ravish Tiwari: Why are those outside the government demanding your resignation?

I am not here to defend myself. Why is it necessary to discuss this issue?

•Ritu Sarin: Do you think it is unfair to attack you, alone, whenever there is a terror attack?

This criticism has not disturbed my equanimity. People are entitled to their opinions. I am blessed to be able to bear criticism. If I was not, I would not have remained calm. In the last two months, I haven't experienced a single tense moment.

•Ritu Sarin: The government has a huge shopping list for the modernisation of its security and intelligence set up. Is there a political will to implement this or is financial clearance a stumbling block?

I have never had any difficulty while dealing with the Finance Minister or any other cabinet minister. But if you expect things to be done in a day or two, there is a problem. Our system is such you cannot immediately act upon a decision. Things have to be conceptualised. Then they have to be left to the administration for implementation. The process takes time. If things are not done in the right manner, you will land up in a soup later on. But I have never had any problem in getting anything done. People are not acquainted with our plans, policies and projects to strengthen the intelligence agencies, modernise them, provide better transport and communication facilities. These moves have been going on for several years. It is only once you know these details that you will be in a position to question whether we are doing enough. The media doesn't have the time to understand all the details and we don't have the time to explain it all. Thus, a communication gap is created, leading to criticism from many quarters.

•Shekhar Gupta: There has been a breakthrough in the recent blasts that ties everything to one group. Are you confident that this breakthrough is genuineallegations that the Jamia Nagar encounter in Delhi is fake have led to demands for a judicial inquiry?

The current breakthrough is a good success but we need to do more. As for Jamia Nagar, at this stage, I cannot say whether I have any doubts or not. You have to examine the evidence before coming to a conclusion. It is our duty though to convince people that we would not take an unjust stand. I have never said that what the police did was wrong or right. The executive cannot pass a judgment. You cannot expect me to say whether it was fake or not for it will be interpreted in different ways. However, people make demands without understanding things. A judicial inquiry takes up to five years and even after that you cannot punish someone on the basis of that inquiry. An investigation, filing a charge sheet and the court's judgment together can take up to 10 years. There is an investigation in progress and the matter will be transferred to the court. If the court says it is wrong, then the people who have done it will be held responsible.

•Sobhana K.: People are holding rallies protesting against the encounter but your government is not ready to back your own police. The police force is very angry, it feels abandoned.

I do not think the police misunderstand the government. There is a procedure, let it be followed. If some people have doubts, it is our duty to convince them that we will not adopt wrong methods to defend ourselves or to unnecessarily harass others. We would like to be as correct as possible and that is exactly what we are doing. People say I am very soft on terrorwhat do they mean? Should I go on shouting about the matter? Should I contradict them every now and again? If an occasion arises where dialogue ceases to work and the state has to act, it will do so. On the other hand, deciding that a certain section of the society is solely responsible for a terrorist incident and proceeding against them is not correct. I am not going to form an opinion on the basis of hearsay.

•Shekhar Gupta: Was Inspector M.C. Sharma a hero?

Why should we ask these questions? If he has died in the service of the nation how can we say he has not done his duty unless it is proved otherwise? I went to his funeral, offered flowers, sympathised with his family and unless it is proved otherwise, I do not want to degrade him or his memory. I do not know how many people actually knew Sharma closely, but everyone is now forming opinions and raising questions about him.

•Seema Chishti: There seems to be a lack of clarity on this at the political level. Both those who believe Inspector Sharma is a martyr and those who think Muslims are being targeted because they are Muslim, are annoyed with your government. Aren't you falling between two stools? You don't seem to be making statements to command the middle ground?

People say we are targeting Muslims only. They do not know that we have banned many organisations that belong to different communities. There are approximately 24 such organisations in different states that have been banned. Are we not proceeding against the Naxalites and do they not comprise members of different communities? At the National Integration Council meeting last week, the PM explained the government's policy. There is no lack of clarity on that. We would like to see that innocents are not harassedthere is no ambiguity in our minds on that. We are not saying all Muslims are terrorists. There have been instances when Hindus have taken up armsthat does not mean that all Hindus are terrorists. We would not do anything simply on the basis of caste, community or religion.

•Raghvendra Rao: At the NIC meeting, you reiterated that the existing anti terror laws are adequate. So has the government abandoned the idea of a new anti-terror law?

Let's look at laws like MISA, TADA, POTA which have been repealed. The Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act (MACOCA) came into existence and continues to exist in Maharashtra. I was an MP when TADA was repealed. At the time, we were in the Opposition and asked why it was being repealed. The government of the day said because it was being used to keep people behind bars for long periods. The same charge was leveled against POTA. But when POTA was repealed, we transferred some chapters from it to the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act. These included chapters on protection of innocents from terrorist acts, transfer of funds from one organisation to another or one country to another, making admissible in court the evidence collected by electronic methods, telephonic conversations, etc., the provision relating to the immunity offered to officers who acted against terrorists with a bonafide intention. The Unlawful Activities Act is a law that can be used to control terrorist activities. What we have objected to is the admissibility of a confession given to the police as evidence in court and shifting the onus from the prosecution to the defence for proving guilt, as this goes against the basic tenets of criminal jurisprudence. We have also amended the CrPC on the basis of reports from the Law Commission. As for Maharashtra, it has MACOCA; yet it is affected by terrorist attacks. The law by itself cannot help. But a law is important and should be amended when required.

•Shekhar Gupta: If Maharashtra can have this law, then why are you not clearing similar laws for BJP-ruled states?

When TADA was repealed, the then Chief Minister of Maharashtra brought MACOCA into existence. It was not a Congress government that enacted the law. If Gujarat wants to pass such a law, it can do so without the permission of the Government of India. I cannot ask the state to repeal a law. In the Gujarat law and in MACOCA, there are provisions like those in POTA. Can the executive approve of provisions that were repealed by it? POTA said that confessions made to the police should be made admissible as evidence. But POTA was repealed because of such provisions, so how can I let Gujarat pass a law with such provisions? If such provisions are taken out of the law, there is no problem in approving it.

•Ritu Sarin: There are 40 people on death row and 26 cases are pending. Has President Patil reviewed or discussed any death row cases with you?

I cannot discuss these matters. They are privileged.

•Vinay Sitapati: Health Minister Anbumani Ramadoss and NACO have provided evidence that decriminalising homosexuality would prevent AIDS. So why has the Home Ministry filed an affidavit before the Delhi High Court saying that it will actually increase the spread of AIDS?

A law has to be acceptable to people if it is to be effective. You cannot implement a law because it has the government's sanction. But tell me, how many cases have we actually filed to prosecute people for homosexuality? There are no such cases pending in the court except those where children are victims of sexual abuse.

•Coomi Kapoor: Were you hurt when the Left vetoed your name for President?

I would not like to defend myself nor would I want to say that something wrong was done to me. My countrymen and my party have given me much more than I deserve.

•Ravish Tiwari: Now that the government is ready for elections, what do you as Home Minister have to flaunt as successes?

Between 1999-2004, the number of incidents in J&K, the North-East and the Naxal-affected states, and incidents of communal violence was 36,000. The number for the period 2004-2008 is 25,000. The number of civilian casualties for this period has come down from 11,000 to about 6,000. Yet, we are told that the situation has worsened.

Transcribed by Ayesha Arvind

Heading: The dark ink - Indian Express
Content:
The painter from Kovalam, Babu Xavier, belies the myth that the artist is only a superstar
Nestled as it is in a verdant coconut grove on Kovalam beach in Kerala, Babu Xavier's studio does not resemble the state-of-the-art spaces of many artists in metros. His attire (a pair of trousers and a bush shirt) and networking skills (or the lack thereof) don't have the mark of urban panache. But, here's the surprise: his art reflects none of the provincial concerns of typical Kerala artists; it is nothing if not international.

"My reason to paint never came from reality. My inspiration comes from literature and media. Some of my images come from a sense of play, others from deeper concerns about modern life," says Xavier, whose early Marxist leanings played a major role in shaping his ideology. "When I portray the landscape of my homeland, it's not with the intention of presenting a pastoral or beautiful view. For me, beauty lies in the metaphor of the object or the vista; I love to render it in a manner which is surreal," says the artist.

After his August solo show, Organic Dreams, at Triveda Art Gallery in Delhi, Xavier brings a new body of work, Printer's Horror Series, a collection of silk screen prints and acrylics on canvas that is being showcased at the Jehangir Art Gallery, Mumbai. "This show is different from anything I have done, since it sources images directly from media and transforms them into ponderings over their backstage life," he says.

Xavier is a self-taught painter and has evolved a style quite different from academic or photo-realism common in Kerala artists. He has used popular ads like the Virgin mobile phone that has a leggy lass as its brand ambassador. "The word virgin appearing in the composition assumes an all together different meaning since it mentally connects the viewer with the image of the Virgin Mary. The paradox lies in the fact that it ironically points to the burden of virginity in an urbanised and liberated modern society," writes P Surendran, Malayali writer and chronicler of these artwork.  

Xavier uses his brand of black humour well and gets his point across without being preachy or taking himself too seriously. After all, even his pricing is more realistic than many of his contemporaries. "I would want as many people as possible to enjoy my art. And if I out-price myself, only a few collectors will afford me, which is why I have tried to keep it real," he says. Xavier's acrylics on canvas go for around Rs 2 lakh, while his paper works are priced around Rs 60,000. The inclusion of a bar code signature (which was then copied by many artists) indicates that Xavier is well aware of the commoditisation of art. "Anyway, prices in the market are quite lopsided. There is more value for me now abroad," he adds.  

For those who do not know how the magic began, Xavier had humble beginnings.
It was 1985 when a honeymooning couple, holidaying in Kovalam, chanced upon his postcard sized paintings and approached Mario Miranda to advise them. "Mario liked my work and recommended they buy it. That incident gave me the confidence to begin working seriously," says Xavier. His middle-class family had expected him to study medicine or engineering. "They were all surprised when I told them I was becoming an artist," says Xavier with a smile and a chuckle. Twenty-three-years later, as he stands in Jehangir Art Gallery filled with interested buyers, art students and viewers, he knows he made the right decision. 

Six months after he was 'discovered', Xavier made a trip to Mumbai. He chanced upon Dadiba Pundole's art gallery Pundole at Flora Fountain, Mumbai. There, he met a very encouraging gallery manager Pramila K. She saw his small format watercolours, and confidently suggested a solo show at Pundole. The show was a sellout, and it established Xavier as an artist with a bright future. Since then, he has not looked back.

"When I began painting, it was not a profession that had this much money in it. I did it because I felt I had something to say to the world. Now my daughter teases me by saying she too will become a painter and earn lots of money," says Xavier, every bit the family man.

Having met his wife in an unusual situation, Xavier wanted to live out his life according to Marxist ideals. She was a construction worker and the image of her breaking stones on the roadside was poetic and yet heroic. Xavier married her after a brief courtship and the two have set up a farm near their coconut plantation, both of which are flourishing along with his career as an artist.

"Somehow I can never live in a city; my brief visits to Mumbai and Delhi have shown me that," chuckles Xavier. "I feel connected enough through email and television and the newspapers," he adds.

Besides the media-inspired works, Xavier has embarked on a series of imaginative and almost hallucinogenic images of hybrid animals, fantasy landscapes and human beings. They are all drenched in colours that are bright and bold and yet there is no attempt to pretty things up. "Fantasy is very important to my works. I believe it is a universal expression," says the artist, feet firmly on the ground.

Heading: BUD WISER - Indian Express
Content:
Graphic novelist Sarnath Banerjee has 'internalised' the mysterious story-telling of Edgar Allan Poe
It's a difficult proposition to pin down one particular book I can call a classic. I've always been inclined towards crime fiction and Edgar Allan Poe's Collection of Short Stories is one piece of literature that has kept me hooked ever since I first read in it 1990—when I was studying in Class XI. I keep going back to the book now and then in bits and parts, though I must have read the complete book at least seven times. I wouldn't say that Poe's prose inspires my literary style but, yes, some of its ramifications have certainly been internalised by me.

Poe was the master of creating a gothic atmosphere—through his description of the dreary landscape, the haunted house, the mysterious illness and the eerie mood—thus causing a feeling of utter dread that had the power to seep deep inside your bones. And though his occult tales were highly uncanny and thrilling, they were subtle and toned-down too.

Poe was the father of modern-day detective stories and his central character, Augustine Dupin, was a precursor to the creation of later detective legends such as Sherlock Holmes. His stories inspired not only novelists such as Sir Arthur Conan Doyle who created Holmes but also contemporary filmmakers such as David Lynch whose films  Mulholland Drive (2001) and Eraserhead (1977) have drawn their surreal/mysterious elements from Poe's works.

Among the short stories of Poe, I particularly like The Fall of the House of Usher which is an exemplary gothic tale. It's about an old, decrepit house in Scotland whose owner, Roderick Usher, is ill and scared and thus asks his friend to stay with him. It turns out that the house is spooky and the owner is afraid of it. The story revolves around the cursed estate. The description of its structure and atmosphere almost makes the building a personality in itself—a literary feat. It's the kind of story that would enchant any thinking, creative person—a novelist or a graphic designer or a filmmaker. And it definitely enchants me.

Heading: Eye spy - Indian Express
Content:
What are the chances of miserably failing in plucking dead petals off 15 roses in 15 minutes? As it turned out — fairly high. Twenty minutes past—and I was still trying to figure out the dead ones from the fresh. My guide Siddharth Kharath of Shamun's flower shop on MG Road in Pune was not amused by my expertise. Watching me fumble way past the deadline, Kharath said, "There is very little difference between a fresh and a dead petal in these buds. You have to have an eye for that," he said, not bothering to even thinly disguise his disillusionment.  

Eager to please, I took out yet another petal from the rose in my hand, which according to my discretion was a 'dead' one and darted a glance at Kharath. Wonder of wonders, he nodded. "This time you got it right. Otherwise, you have been plucking fresh petals all this while," he said.

But the joy was short-lived. "We already have wasted so much time on such a small thing. The main process begins now. You will learn how to make a simple arrangement for bouquets." Okay, this sounded easy after the tedious process of plucking fresh-looking dead petals from roses, I muttered to myself.

But as he went about explaining the so-called simple arrangement of the bouquet, my heart sank. "One straight rose between two crossed roses. Don't forget that the roses should be at the same level. Your hold should neither be tight nor loose. Position the roses close together so that their arrangement is symmetrical and all the roses are visible." My God! Is he ever going to pause? I wondered.

I tried to imagine all the lovely rose bouquets I have seen till date, and get my task right. "This way you won't be able to hold even these three roses properly, forget 15. Grip the stems very lightly, with four of your fingers holding it from one side, and just the thumb gripping it from the other side." I observed my own grip and noticed the clumsy arrangement of my fingers. "I was just wondering if the stems have thorns," I blurted out in my defense. He smiled sweetly, "Some of them do have thorns. Just be careful."

The lesson continued. "Now instead of one straight rose put two in between two crossed roses and put the ferns on both the straight roses. This will give the bouquet a circular look, also see the roses are at the same level. That is very important," he said.

After arranging another row like the previous one I came back to the first pattern of one straight rose. As the cello tape circled the stems I looked towards Kharath. "You just took longer than usual in making it. The arrangement is fine. Now we have a basket bouquet pending. It is an elaborate arrangement but the process is simple because you have to place them in the punch oasis instead of your hands. So both your hands are free," he said cheering me up. 

Numbers, he said, are all one has to keep in mind while making a basket bouquet. " Three and five for the first two rows." So I tried to imitate Kharath who took three gladiolas in his hand measured them and cut one of them around two inches short than the other two. Then he placed it on the punch oasis with two gladiolas on one level and the middle one slightly lower. And then came the line of roses, which he arranged like stairs. Next came white carnations that were punched even on the sides of the punch oasis. After that came the turn of some greens as fillers for which he used asparagus fern.

In my enthusiasm, I picked the fern promptly. But he warned, "Watch out it has sharp thorns." But the warning came too late. The lively green had gotten a red bob of blood on my thumb. Who knew even a florist's job had such occupational hazards!

What also took my mind away from the pain was the fact that my efforts were beginning to bear fruit—or should it be flowers?  I gave the fern its due respect and placed it carefully in the punch. And as I finished, Kharath smiled and said "Good job!" Now that was something! I started imagining running my own florist business.

"Now you can go down and deliver the bouquet to the customer," Kharath's voice jolted me out of my reverie. "The customer is downstairs. You are supposed to deliver it to him." I approached the customer with my bouquet in hand. I sensed his eyes examining the bouquet closely. I kept thinking, "He is going to reject it, I know. There are many flaws, the greens are not aligned properly, the roses are not at the right level." After a minute he asked, "I have to pay Rs 300 for it, right?" My heart jumped with joy.
"I will miss that bouquet," I said to Kharath. He just rolled his eyes and went back to the bunch of orchids waiting for him.

Heading: A scottish affair - Indian Express
Content: Fashion designers are shifting focus to the eyes. They are getting bigger and brighter. Christian Dior and Miu Miu have experimented with bold colours for the eyes in their collection. Colours such as lime green, sky blue, fuschia pink, yellow, and purple are in. Manish Arora, who has recently tied up with MAC for a make-up collection, says "Everything is eyes is big, from extra-long lashes to a mix of wacky colours." In designer Kavita Bhartia's show, models walked the ramp wearing colourful eyelashes. "The look was very adventurous," she says. Arora's make up line has shades to go with every skin tone. However, this look is only for those who are willing to experiment. "It's a trendy look and is for those who want to have fun with make-up," says make up artist Mickey Contractor.

Heading: Problem of plenty - Indian Express
Content:
You can't bet on the Highland sun but in Beauly, a village in Scotland, medieval monasteries and spectacular wildlife make for a holiday to remember
In scotland, you never have enough time for the beauty around you. Here I was, waking up to the plaintive cries of seagulls at a guesthouse in Inverness one morning when the next beautiful destination, 12 miles away, beckoned. Don, our driver, was waiting for us impatiently as we got into the van and headed for the scenic village of Beauly. On our way, we passed through Lochinver, with its fabulous braes and huge swathes of wilderness. The day before, I had thought that I had seen all there was to of the magnificent Highlands. But the route to Beauly proved me wrong at every corner.

Beauly is a bustling village that should be explored by foot. In the 13th century, Cistercian monks built a priory here, deciding that Beauly was the ideal spot for their secluded meditation and worship. The area's beauty has even gotten it some royal compliments. In 1564, Mary, Queen of Scots, stopped at Beauly Priory on her way to Easter Ross. Touched by the beauty of the priory, she is reputed to have said in French, "Oui, c'est un beau lieu" (Yes, it is a beautiful place), a pun on the name of the priory.

Beauly's market square has shops lined with travel rugs or blankets in tartans and check designs in both wool and mohair. You can also stock up on luxurious scarves and sweaters in cashmere and lambswool from well-known brands such as Pringle and Ballentyne. Our genial and witty driver Don regaled us with tales of his childhood in the Trossachs as we drove towards Beinn Eighe National Nature Reserve.

Sunshine can never be guaranteed in the Highlands, but visitors over the years have become used to donning wellies and having a great day out, whatever weather comes their way. Luckily for us, there was plenty of sunshine at the nature reserve which is an ancient pine forest overlooking Loch Maree. It is also home to a multitude of spectacular wildlife, including red deer and the golden eagle.

Any holidaymaker with an eye for nature would be overjoyed with the abundance of flora and fauna that the Highlands offer. Spring is the best time to see the many species of wild flowers which bloom in the glens and leafy avenues while among the feathered residents you may find song thrushes, dippers, buzzards, herons and, with luck, a Peregrine falcon or two. Early evenings and early mornings are also the best times to see families of shy badgers or wily country foxes. Don gave us an excellent book on the birds of the Highlands, which we thumbed through trying to identify the birds we saw perched on trees around us.

There was more excitement in store as we took one of the highest roads in Scotland — to Bealach na Ba, the Pass of the Cattle. It is said to be the steepest road in Britain and provides breathtaking views of Alpine grandeur. Don skillfully drove past the hairpin bends and precipitous cliffs which made up the only road linking Applecross with the rest of the country until the late 20th century. Applecross, whose Gaelic name, a'Chomraich, translates as 'the sanctuary,' dates back to the building of a monastery by an Irish monk in the area in the seventh century. Today, nothing remains of the ancient monastery of St Maelrubha. Its site is marked by the much more recent Old Parish Church at Craig, built in 1818, near the north side of the bridge over what is now called the River Applecross.

No holiday picture or album of Scotland is complete without a photograph of a hairy Highland cow. They are as much a recognised tourist symbol of Scotland as tartan, heather, kilts and bagpipes. These cows are formidable looking beasts, yet they are known to be peaceful, content and docile. We were fortunate to be able to take snaps of one that was sleeping blissfully in a field a few miles from Applecross. A signboard next to the field said his name was Hamish and that he was 15 years old. Our driver told us that he had once been invited to the inauguration of a superstore as the 'chief guest'. Sadly, he ate the ribbon after it had been cut!

If you want to take a Highland cow or two home with you to graze the lawn, you can get one at the main markets at Oban in the months of February and October. But be prepared to dig deep into your bank account. A good pedigree Highland bull reportedly costs in the region of £10,000 while a 'hairy Heilan coo' may set you back by £5,000.

I decided against getting a Highland cow, but after the feast for the eyes, my stomach wanted pampering. Last stop: a fantastic dinner of grilled salmon rolls at the Isle of Skye under a startlingly pure, pale blue sky.

Heading: Living with pco D - Indian Express
Content:
What Next?
Chris Patten
Allen Lane, Rs 795

Chris Patten surveys the challenges of the millennium, but is profoundly ambivalent about many issues
What next? is an engagingly written and fair-minded tour d' horizon of the principal challenges facing the world: the pooling of sovereignty, inequality, nuclear proliferation, the spread of small arms, civil wars and natural-resource conflicts, water, organised crime and money laundering, drugs, the looming energy crisis, global warming, pandemics, enemies of freedom. The narrative is clear, elegant, often enriched with a deep sense of history and irony, enlivened with a telling fact. In some ways, this book is distinct from many others of its genre, in not having an overarching thesis or a simple, structural story to tell, and often it hedges its own conclusions. In many respects, this is a great advantage.

Patten does not flatten the world, the sectoral focus brings to attention the vulnerabilities and challenges that often get short shrift in more grandiose narratives. But this virtue is also a vice, in that each of these can appear to be a series of discrete problems, ripe for separate interventions. While Patten occasionally gestures at the interconnections between them, there is an overwhelming sense, in the way the book is written, that each of these problems occupies its own separate domain; that they are not systematically linked. In that sense, the book fosters an illusion that each problem (with the exception of drugs) is available for a "technical" intervention if only we had the will to do it. In some instances, these problems then become disembedded from the societies from which they emerge, as if "organised crime", for instance, is the same everywhere. Much of what Patten has to say is quite sensible — strengthen nuclear proliferation, control small-arms trade, promote peace in the Middle East. Some proposals are bold but vague, as on climate change: "This means putting aside thoughts of a worldwide anti-carbon dictatorship which would move remorselessly from controlling every carbon footprint to trying to control the number of the world's feet, in other words how much we are allowed to breed."

Patten is also even handed in his judgments: not afraid to criticise his own government. But there is often a sense that this criticism is more a gesture than genuine self correction. For instance, he is tempted by the idea of nuclear disarmament, passes some strictures on the hypocrisy of the nuclear world order, and is profoundly ambivalent about the Indo-US nuclear deal. But in the end he leaves the crucial question hanging: what will be the drivers of making nuclear weapons illegitimate? What justifies Britain upgrading its arsenal? He discusses the banking crisis, and locates its sources in, among other things, poor regulation. But there is little discussion of the ideological and political currents that led to poor regulation, currents which Patten had a ringside view of.

But there are often two problems with such wide-ranging narratives. First, they tend to be more of rumination than a rigorous argument, gesturing at the complexity of the issues without internalising it. Second, and perhaps more seriously, they take the vantage point of view of a legislator of the world, someone surveying from a high-up perch the various follies and foibles of mankind. From this vantage point, the solutions all seem clear and Patten does not hesitate to propose many. The only thing lacking of this view is that mysterious entity called "political will", as if setting history right were simply a matter of will.

At one level, Patten's historical sensibility is quite admirable. He is closer to what in the eighteenth century would have been described as a sceptical Whig, someone who believes progress is possible, but does not believe that it unfolds according to a predetermined logic. Indeed, often its sources are unexpected. He believes in political creativity, understands the limits of reason, powerfully articulates the view that often things go wrong not because we aim to do ill, but because we have romantic conceptions of the good. His account of human motivation is complex: it is not reduced to simple self interest. Instead, pride, fear and a whole range of passions play their part. His heroes are not idealists, they are Metternich and Talleyrand, once dismissed as reactionaries, now acknowledged as realists who kept the worst excesses of virtue and ideological purity at bay. The disappointment of the book is that Patten's analysis of problems is often at odds with his own understanding of politics; indeed the political questions remain unexamined. Like Talleyrand, Patten rightly thinks that change will come, not from idealists, but from people who can cut deals. Whether for the world or for themselves remains an open question.

Heading: Sweet Dreams - Indian Express
Content:
Healthy eating and regular exercise can help you fight polycystic ovarian disease
Twenty-four-year-old Anshu Ghai's menstrual cycle had been irregular for six months before she finally decided to see a doctor. "My period would last for two weeks and then start again in a week or 10 days," she says. After an ultrasound, she found that she was suffering from polycystic ovary disease (PCOD), a condition in which cysts are formed in both ovaries and no egg is released every month. The symptoms of this disease are irregular periods with heavy bleeding or no bleeding at all.

The root cause of PCOD is unknown. It is a lifetime female hormonal imbalance where maturing eggs fail to be expelled from the ovary, creating an ovary filled with immature follicles (also called cysts). High insulin levels somehow boost the production of androgens and testosterone which prevent the ovaries from releasing an egg each month. "The cysts then cause a hormonal imbalance, which causes more cysts, it is like a vicious cycle," says Dr Rinku Sengupta, gynaecologist, Sitaram Bhartia Research Institute.

PCOD may also be hereditary. "Women with a family history of PCOD are 50 per cent more likely to develop it," say Dr Sengupta. "The most common risk is infertility. Since this condition affects young women, it is the most bothersome as well," says Dr Raj Bukari, gynaecologist, Fortis La Femme. About half the women affected by PCOD also gain weight and the condition increases the risk of high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol, type 2 diabetes and problems related to the liver and heart.

The condition is most common among women who have just started menstruating or women in their early 20s. Once you have been diagnosed with PCOD, no treatment will take it away completely. However, hormonal treatments and a healthy lifestyle will make it better. "When we get a patient suffering from PCOD, we give them hormone supplements to deal with the imbalance in the body. Our first concern is to make sure that the patient is able to conceive. Mostly with treatment, they are," says Dr Bukari. She adds, "The hormone supplements vary from person to person and must only be taken with a doctor's prescription."

While treatment will dissolve or remove the cysts from the ovaries, it is a condition that will keep recurring every few years. So, a change in lifestyle is very important. Doctors say PCOD has only become common amongst young women in the past 10 years. "Earlier, we had very few cases of women with a hormonal imbalance or polycystic ovaries. Now, the numbers have risen. Five out of ten patients come to me complaining of irregular periods, as compared to the one in ten earlier," says Dr Sengupta. Blaming lifestyle changes, she says, "Women work till late hours, eat a lot of junk, don't exercise, smoke, consume alcohol and lead stressful lives." In some cases, PCOD gets better after pregnancy.

Even if one is undergoing hormonal treatment, exercise and a healthy diet is important to keep it under control. Eat lots of vegetables and fresh fruits. "Avoid junk food and sweets. Also, avoid binge eating. Eat small meals," says Dr Sengupta. Since PCOD is related with obesity, patients must exercise to increase metabolism and keep sugar levels low. "Thirty minutes of exercise daily is the minimum one should do," she adds.

Heading: ‘I eat seven small meals a day’ - Indian Express
Content:
It's common to occasionally not be able to fall asleep through the night due to stress and indigestion. But difficulty in falling asleep or maintaining sleep or not getting restorative sleep for more than a month means you're having chronic insomnia. Common causes include stress, certain medical conditions, lifestyle changes, exercising before bedtime, consumption of alcohol, caffeine and large meals. Besides lowering productivity, inadequate sleep also carries the following risks:

Weight Gain
Studies have shown that sleeping only four hours for two consecutive nights decreases levels of hunger-suppressing hormone (leptin) and increases levels of hunger-promoting hormone (ghrelin). A new research in Germany has found that this increase in ghrelin levels may occur after just one night of inadequate sleep.

Insulin resistance and Diabetes
Studies have shown lack of sleep induces insulin resistance, which means more insulin is needed to store an amount of glucose. Less than five hours of sleep at night may increase the risk of developing type 2 diabetes by 2.5 times. On the other hand, sleeping for nine hours or more too may increase diabetes risk.

Heart Disease
Research has shown that less than five hours of sleep at night on a regular basis may increase the risk of heart disease. Both conditions—'too little' and 'too much' sleep —may increase production of stress hormones, leading to high blood pressure. Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart disease.

Accidents
Insomnia may cause poor concentration and thus increase the risk of accidents. Daytime sleepiness also increases worker's risk of injury at work.

Sleeping Pills
The pills may cause rebound insomnia i.e. falling asleep takes longer after their consumption has been discontinued.

Diet influences our sleep in a big way and incorporating the following dietary modifications can be a help:
*Avoid large meals before sleeping as they may lead to discomfort when lying down and make it difficult to sleep. Some people also experience heartburn—backflow of acid and food from the stomach into the esophagus—after eating, and this can cause discomfort when lying low. Finish your last meal at least two hours before bedtime.
*Watch your intake of alcohol as it interrupts with sleep sequence and duration, and makes one wake earlier. Slow down on caffeine as it blocks sleep-inducing chemicals in the brain and increases adrenaline production. Also, caffeine being a diuretic (increases passage of urine) will cause disturbances due to increased waking.
*Take tryptophan-containing foods such as low-fat milk, banana, nuts, seeds, soya and greens before bedtime as tryptophan is needed to make sleep-inducing substances, serotonin and melatonin.
*A recent Iranian study found that salt disrupts normal sleep pattern and decreases the duration of deep sleep. Avoid high-salt foods like pickles, chutneys, papads, chips, salted nuts and other preserved and processed foods in the last hours of the day.
*Consume most of your water in the earlier part of the day. Having excessive water at night means increased need to wake up and may disrupt sleep. This is particularly true with elderly and those with medical problems.

Exercise regularly—at least three hours before bedtime—to relieve stress and thus work towards good sleep. Go to bed at the same time each night. This will work best to set circadian rhythms.
While sleep requirements vary considerably among people, most need about seven to eight hours of sleep a night.

Heading: ‘I’m living in with my self, single and happy’ - Indian Express
Content:
KOENA MITRA, ACTRESS

Tell us about your daily diet
I eat six to seven meals a day—all in small portions. For instance, a bowl of six egg whites with a glass of juice would make one meal. After a break of four hours, it would be porridge with a piece of chicken. Another four-hour break and it's fruits. Dinner is white meat or roasted chicken. I avoid sweets and milk products.

What's your exercise routine?
I work out five days a week and do only weight training as it helps tone my body. I am not fond of yoga or cardio since they get boring after a while.

What's your favourite cuisine?
I am a more of a non-vegetarian and love anything to do with meat, which is high on protein. I also love grilled fish.

Is there anything you binge on?
Bhel Puri—it's fat-free, spicy and tasty.
What would you do if you had to put on or lose weight in a hurry?
I'll modify the proportion of food I take and the workout plan accordingly. For putting on weight, I'll eat more and exercise less. For losing, it would be 70 per cent workout and 30 per cent food.

How many times have you failed to stick to a diet?
To be honest, I am not a foodie. I eat because it is a necessity and is required to survive. So, it's not difficult for me to stick to a diet.

What's your idea of health?
A healthy mind, a healthy diet and a healthy lifestyle.

Heading: Smash hits - Indian Express
Content:
The actress on being a woman's woman, cricket, films and Vikram Bhatt

Why did you decide to become a judge on the reality show, Ek Khiladi Ek Haseena (EKEH)?
It's a unique show which would be difficult to put together again in the future, what with the participation of cricketers who form the playing eleven and getting approval from the BCCI. The producers agreed that I won't do drama for TRPs and will not rip apart the contestants. The money was great and since it's a 10-episode show, I was required for only five days.  

But do you watch television?
Not as much as I'd like to. But since my daughter, Renee, loves television shows like Nach Baliye and Fear Factor:  Khatron Ke Khiladi, I'm pretty clued in. Renee loves EKEH and wants me to do more such fun stuff.

Does Renee know her mother is a movie star?
She knows that I'm an actress but she perceives me as her friends in school perceive me. She tells me that her friends liked a song of mine and that they liked me on TV. But I must tell you that Renee has a pretty definite idea of what I should or shouldn't do on screen. She doesn't like me playing sobbing characters. She didn't like Vaastu Shastra and was adamant I never do scary films again. She wants me to do films like Main Hoon Na and Samay.

Do you follow cricket?
I was addicted to the IPL. I like Twenty20 and 50-over one-days but can't sit through a Test. As for my favourite cricketers, it's a toss-up between Mahendra Singh Dhoni, Irfan Pathan and Shane Warne.

Wasim Akram says your Urdu is better than his.
(Smiles) Masha Allah! I love the tehzeeb of Urdu. Bengali and French are sweet while Punjabi is powerful but Urdu is one language that treats every emotion with respect. Urdu mein gaali bhi poetry lagti hai (Even an abuse in Urdu sounds like poetry). I also like shaiyari and hope to write my poems in Urdu, not English.   

Your film outings have reduced considerably. Why is that?
I've been here for a decade, doing experimental films. Now, I want to do projects that really excite me. I want to do good, commercial and big-banner films like Main Hoon Na that offer big publicity. I just want to entertain my audience and then take my hat off.  

What's the status of your much-hyped films like Dulha Mil Gaya and Karma, Confessions and Holy?
Well, it's really sad that Dulha Mil Gaya is stuck. I've played a dolled up caricature in it. We just need 10 days with Shah Rukh Khan and then we'd be done. As for Karma…, I've no idea. I took offence to a teaser on the Internet which misrepresented the film. Let's just hope for the best. In my life, nothing has come without waiting. But I don't fret since the results more than make up for the wait.

What's the status of your dream, Jhansi Ki Rani?
Let me clarify once and for all that it's not Jhansi Ki Rani. My film is the story of a woman who was the queen of Jhansi and so it's called Rani Laxmi Bai. If the title changes, so does the story. We're through with the scripting. It's in the storyboard stage. It's not an easy film to make—what with it being expensive, historical and woman-oriented. Ask anyone in the industry and they'll tell you it's a bad idea. I didn't choose this film, it chose me.  

Won't talking about the film before its shooting begins make it stale?
(Ponders) You're right. The way everybody is going on about it, you'd think it's being shot right now. People have to realise that I don't want to make it a 'by-the-way' film. Rani Laxmi Bai is the biggest I've dreamt. I want to plan it so well on paper that I don't have any problems while shooting it. If I'm taking my time, it's because I don't want to mess it up. The media should let the film breathe.  

Are you still keen to direct it?
As of now, yes. Shekhar Kapur told me that since I see it so clearly, there's no way anybody else can direct it. It's going to be tough but I'll attempt it. Rest assured, my production house will come out with at least three more films before that.

Is it true you approached Salman Khan for a role in Rani Laxmi Bai?
Yes. But Salman is already doing a historical epic, Veer. I've seen his dates and he has no time to breathe. He just couldn't accommodate the film.

Does a friend saying no to you affect the friendship?
No. It's better to have a friend say no than to keep you hanging. Salman is still and will always be a friend.

You've always been perceived to be a woman's woman. Do you agree?
The biggest blessing I get is when women come up to me and appreciate me. Some women have told me that they are happy that their husbands like me. I've never entered a room and faced hostility, envy or jealousy from any woman. I've had this relationship with them since I was 18. And that's why whenever the media unleashes a character analysis of me, I don't react. I tell my Baba there are people out there whom I've never met who believe in me. I haven't gone out to create any opinion about me.

So, speculations about your personal life don't bother you?
They did when I was younger. But I've learned from my and others' lives that everything is transient. When you're on a high—everyone around you goes ga ga—and when you hit a low, everyone pretends to not know you. When you realise this fact, you stop fighting. Fighters know when to lie low, they stand up and fight when the time is right.

Recent reports suggest that you're living in with Dulha Mil Gaya director, Mudassar Aziz.
I'm living in with myself. I'm single and very happy. The media shouldn't jump to conclusions every time I express respect and admiration for a human being.

Are you aware that Vikram Bhatt who earlier made a film on you, Ankahee, is now writing a book on his past relationships?
Yeah, I read about it. It doesn't bother me. Normally, people are afraid of their life being recounted in a book or a film because they have something to hide. My life has been so beautiful, I don't fear anything. He is writing about his experiences. He's a free man and can do whatever he wants. I've realised that I can't take responsibility for others' actions. God bless his book.

Heading: Hamburg House - Indian Express
Content:
A sport shorn of glitz is giving us our new heroes. And leading the charge of badminton's stars is one gritty girl, Saina Nehwal
Now that Saina Nehwal has put it so matter-of-factly, seems strange that in my five years of some aggressive Harry Potter proselytising, not one fan of the book-series ever confessed to the Potter-boy being their favourite character. "Harry, obviously," said India's fast-rising badminton starin the course of a rapid-fire barrage of quick questions, quicker answers. Politely too, for she's not the sorts who'll say 'D-uh!' to such questions.

Too busy peeling life's many layers, making heroes out of a Ron or a Hermione or Fred, essentially the support-cast in the books, we've apparently drifted away from who is central to the plot. Not Nehwal though.
To shuttle-muggles, the 18-year-old is at No 11, on the cusp of entering the world's elite Top 10 of badminton, a zone inhabited by only the supremely athletic and hard-training group of badminton pros. To Potter-ignorants, it'd suffice to say that Nehwal doesn't budge right or left from her goal-path. There's winning, that she considers right; losing, that simply makes her feel wrong. It admittedly made her cry often in the year-long lean period of 2007 when she was getting beaten by the top girls only in her second season then, wondering what she needed to do to get her movements precise and shots right.

Winning her career-high Grand Prix Gold title in Chinese Taipei recently while beating a world champion, within a month of her sterling show at the Olympics where she made an unprecedented appearance for an Indian woman in the quarterfinals, Nehwal is flying high. And admirably not losing sight of the snitch on her own Quidditch patch, if focus is the criterion on which you judge a potential champion. "I'm not the next Prakash Padukone or Gopichand of Indian badminton. I compete in the women's section, no? You can say I'm the best Indian woman shuttler right now," she says, not intending it as a witty retort. Not for the first time, Nehwal is simply stating a fact.

Her definition of fashion is "being simple", cricket is slotted as "entertainment", city-mate Sania Mirza is "star", while analysing herself, Nehwal will giggle and settle for "upcoming star." She was abashed when her father's friend asked her for her first autograph at 15, because she believed she'd not done anything of note (read: beaten a Chinese yet). Now, the youngster believes she's earned the right to scribble her signature. "And also the freedom to shout on court if I get a line-call wrong because I belong up there and I'm there to win," she says. Nehwal says what she's had to give up along the way to making it there was not friends and parties and Sunday brunchesbut her education. "Success hasn't come easy, I've put my studies aside for this," she stresses, her priorities a good pointer to where she comes from.

Minus the TV spotlight which sits easy on tennis, badminton's rise in India will be strictly shorn of glitz and glam. The bling business just doesn't run in parallel lanes to this sport. Frankly, even sleeveless tops are rare on international courts while steadfastly collared shirts among men, are not uncommon.

Unfussed over what she's wearing, and unbothered by whether it all being co-ordinated and matchedas long as it doesn't hamper her mobilityNehwal leads the charge in India's hottest-emerging sport. Her Top 50 contemporaries are the studious Arvind Bhat, an uncomplicated Anup Sridhar, both from Bangalore, and Nehwal's next-rung is Aditi Mutatkar, an equally diligent 20-year-old from an academically-inclined Pune, with her strong beliefs in the hard yards.

Unsurprisingly, the mentors in this success story are former All-England champions Prakash Padukone and P Gopichand, two stand-alone statements of high achievement and simplicity on India's sport-scape, their quotes not intended to be smart and clever, just wise. Even Chetan Anand and Jwala Gutta, dubbed Indian badminton's 'It' couple (Chetan's now India's No. 1, and broke into the 20s with his title in Germany, Jwala picked India's first mixed doubles GP title with V Diju) know the headlines will follow only if they are scaling the high-rankings charts.

Badminton occupies that strange position in Indiaeveryone's played it at picnics and in gardens with non-pricey thin racquets and cheaper plastic substitutes for feather-shuttles, but it never could claim a commensurate share of popular-following. World-over too, the Asian dominance in the last two decades (as against tennis's continued domineering European or American demograph of champions) has meant that prize money on indoor surfaces stayed a fraction of what's offered on clay, grass or hardcourts of tennis. Even its limited TV relays frankly indicate that badminton champions don't really dress or do up for the occasion.

The game with its clutch of young achievers in India hence will take off from a conservative runway of wooden courts, not glitzy ramps. Only, Deepika Padukone might be found oftener court-side for a celebrity match or two, in these changing times.

Father Prakash ruled the courts in his reign of 15 yearsIndian badminton's first golden-periodand ended an exemplary legend for his world-winning ways. This was followed by a slump, before P Gopichand snatched the All-England Badminton Championship in 2001.

Sporadically good performances at the Thomas Cup were more sparkle-sticks, rather than sustained fireworks, before Saina Nehwal stormed onto the scene and re-set the bar. Happily for shuttle, the wings are buzzing too with the likes of P Kashyap, Anand Pawar and Ajay Jayaram hoping to burst onto the main-stage, behind Chetan, Arvind and Anup who are to put up their best shows yet.

"It reminds me of the '80s when the next generation looked strong," says former player and coach Leroy D'Sa. "From our current position, it'd be stupid to go down, because the only way is up. Saina's being modest if she talks of Top 10. It's only a matter of time till she's World No 4, 3, 2 or even 1," he adds. "It's the best time for TV to jump onto the badminton scene. It might not give instant returns, but we need to start telecasting matches on satellite channels. TV channels need to learn to have their rice not just with sambar, the staple cricket, but also with pickle," he remarks.

The challenges though are steep. Nehwal, like others, grapples with the prospect of dealing with China's assembly line of champions day in andday out, before she can demand that kind of visibility and the number of eyeballs on TV. Ad pundit Piyush Pandey sums it best when he says, "Not just as an ad-person, as a mere individual I admire what Nehwal is achieving these days. Unfortunately India's not taken to badminton in a way that Saina's performances would deserve. She's doing her best, but we have to hope the sport itself gets popular if corporates have to seriously consider endorsements and all."

Sports commentator Harsha Bhogle who's always maintained that it is unbecoming of India to be a single-sport country concurs that the girl willat least initiallyhave to try harder than others because of badminton's low and under-stated profile, as against a tennis pro, since the visibility for tennis ensures that even breaking into the Top 50 becomes an event. "Sadly, this has nothing to do with Saina's ability. It is like a fine Bengali actor having to compete with a Hindi film star. It is a measure of the market rather than ability. But if she stays in the Top 10, there'll be a lot of media attention, and some commercial returns," he says.

Hugely impressed with the attitude Nehwal brought to her game, something on display at the Olympics, Bhogle believes the news channels will have a part to play. "Much more than the sports channels where viewership tends to be event-specific," he adds.
She's set the ball rollingthe shuttle whizzing, if you likewhile those like Aditi Mutatkar, who made her first big final recently would be only too happy to walk what is frankly a training torture-path. "I really thank Saina for raising the level, but we all need to work hard to keep the tempo, and get consistent results. Of course, I'll have to kill myself everyday at training, but I want to do that," she says.

Nehwal herself harbours a double-edged fear that keeps her on her toes. "I'm most scared of losing, and I hate the feeling because it affects my confidence," she says. 2007 was a lesson-learnt-fast, and though she escaped the microscope owing to shuttle's modest presence on televisionwhat she wore, how much she weighed wasn't under constant scannerit wasn't without critics screaming, "Loss of focus". "People suggested I'd lost sight of my goal, but I decided I'd keep quiet, and get my racquet to start talking."

For Nehwal, fear assumes the face of the most recent rival who's beaten her more than once. At present, it is Hong Kong's Zhou Mi, whose net-play has wrong-footed the Indian a couple of times. "Besides staying away from fatty food (paneer and naan are her temptation-tests), I think I'm obsessed most with trying to figure her out," she says without subtlety, while narrowing down her challenges.
It's about summoning your patronus, and fending off boggarts, Harry fans would say. For Potter muggles, it means remaining focussed when chasing your goals.
Simply put, it's what Saina Nehwal routinely does.

Heading: Far from Shoreline - Indian Express
Content:
Except for his Yanks, extraordinarily rendered
Would that the American characters in John le Carré's "war-on-terror" novels — Absolute Friends and now A Most Wanted Man — were a little more rounded. Le Carré's Brits and Germans and Chechens and Arabs are defined by the fine-grained complexity that is his authorial trademark. Even Russian Red Army thugs-turned-sleazeball entrepreneurs are allowed shades of white. But American espiocrats seem disappointingly one-dimensional. In le Carré's hands, they wage a war on grammar — "extraordinary rendition of justice" means government-sponsored kidnap, illegal detention and consequences thereof — and are generally unattractive bullies through and through.

In the bleak climax of this beautifully bleak novel, le Carré has one of his Americans say this: "American justice, a******…. Justice from the f****** hip…. Justice with no f****** lawyers around to pervert the course…." I swear, as a compulsive reader and re-reader of le Carré's books, this didn't sound like le Carré. Now, of course, le Carré's moral heft in the war-on-terror novels is directed against what he and many others see as the American state's jihad against rights, decency and logic. This is hugely important and as long as there's terrorism to tackle, a great many critics from all democracies must investigate the manner in which terrorism is tackled. But what may pass muster in politics or activism or journalism, sits poorly in a product of great craftsmanship. It is true, as le Carré is telling us, that one day democracies will look back at this phase of history and count the wrongs committed while doing what had to be done. But le Carré must give us his Yanks more extraordinarily rendered.

Of course, this le Carré has everything else you want from him. 1. Frequently glorious writing: re-read please the few pages devoted to an ex-Islamic militant who has found a second calling as an expert for German Intelligence and who is briefing a bunch of western espiocrats on why an Islamic scholar with a blameless exterior may not wholly be what he seems. 2. A plot that's driven by dialogue where what's not said moves the story forward. 3. The dissection of privileged, diffident, seemingly emotionally challenged Englishness (well, in this book, the protagonist in question is Scottish): George Smiley is obviously the archetype for this novel's Tommy Brue, heir to a failing Germany-based British private bank that has a shady past. There are shades of Barley Blair (The Russia House) and Jerry Westerby (The Honourable Schoolboy) in Brue, as well as those of Alec Leamas (The Spy Who Came in from the Cold), the original le Carré Englishman looking for redemption. 4. The spy who doesn't fit: here, Gunther Bachmann, ex-Intelligence field officer who is somewhat out of favour in Germany's post-9/11, eager-to-be-tough espiocracy.

There's an obligation for the reviewer to give a plot précis. But le Carré really shouldn't be rendered in that fashion. Here's a compromise version. A half-Russian, half-Chechen and fully tortured illegal in Hamburg (the German city where three 9/11 terrorists spent a lot of time and a port city that has always been open to cultural mix) is targeted by German, British and American Intelligence and sought to be protected by a German human-rights lawyer and Brue, the British banker. You should need no more to buy a le Carré.

Final quibbles? Maybe, just maybe, the writing is a bit stretched at times; the Smiley novels seem sparer by comparison and the better for it. And women in recent le Carré novels — Annabel Richter, the German human-rights lawyer, in this one and Tessa Quayle in The Constant Gardener — have been sublimely attractive, essentially good and ultimately unattainable in a way that in effect makes them agents of salvation for conflicted male protagonists.

A woman protagonist in primary le Carré mould and American spies who occasionally suffer from moral qualms — two reasons among many to wait for the next le Carré novel.

Heading: Eating dark chocolate may keep heart healthy - Indian Express
Content:
A gentle story of a singular Konkan family in Chicago
The konkans are the "Jews of India" who knelt before the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama's sword and Saint Francis Xavier's cross, abandoned their Hindu traditions, and became Catholics.

Tony D'Souza's novel shifts between this larger narrative of the Konkan community and a small human drama of an immigrant family in far-flung Chicago. In an almost-anthropological, thick description, it places the story of Francisco D'Sai, his American mother, his Indian father and his beloved uncle Sam in a rich, informing context that has everything from questions of colonialism and its afterlife to minor details of Konkan weddings.

But for all the amplitude of its terrain, what The Konkans does superbly is document the cruelties of a long marriage, which are routinely verbalised and which run too deep for words. The bond between the narrator's parents, Denise and Lawrence, chafes as she yearns for her brief, vivid brush with India, while his life is one long project of American self-fashioning.

Lawrence is obsessed with surfaces and seemliness, and even his concern for the single status of his younger brother Sam stems from a profound standing on ceremony. Sam, by contrast, is an easy-come easy-go second son who never quite falls in love with America, takes the long route to enjoy the trees along the highway, cooks Konkan meals, tells stories and has fitful dreams of returning to India. It is Sam who unstintingly helps an ambitious Indian cousin across, moved by his emotional appeal. When Lawrence tells his son a tale of cheesy uplift, about his grandfather's steely courage assisting the British, Denise and Sam fill in the gory gaps of that story, on how his grandfather made a minor fortune from sandalwood smuggling and exploiting local Hindus. Sam and his sister-in-law are allies, friends and, finally, lovers — and the novel is really the story of their relationship.

To be the first-born Konkan son, Lawrence explains to little Francisco, is a terrible privilege. It is to be responsible forever for the entire family and the weight of their futures. But even as Lawrence is somewhere convinced of his tribal loyalties, he is grudging and wary of the Konkan brood. "Why did I come here if everything I hated about [India] is now dancing in my basement?" he complains about his two brothers.

D'Souza is an expert storyteller — the book opens with a pig slaughter in Chicago, and it brilliantly blends physical comedy and cultural misunderstanding. The hybrid, streetwise atmosphere of the immigrant neighbourhood is also perfectly conveyed. The prose is affecting, and simple.

The Konkans mostly sticks to straight forward storytelling, despite some clunky foreshadowing and some out-of-whack moments when the omniscient, first-person narration fumbles — as Francisco describes his mother's relationship with his uncle, there's some point-of-view disorientation between the young child, the adult narrator and the author. But minor quibbles aside, it is a pleasurable read. It is not a book to go to for light-bulb insight about the immigrant condition, but a gentle and sympathetic story of a pretty singular immigrant family.

Heading: Coming clean on TV - Indian Express
Content:
Eating dark chocolate regularly may help lower levels of inflammation, which is strongly associated with heart and blood vessel disease, researchers report in The Journal of Nutrition. To investigate, they looked at 4,849 healthy men and women participating in an ongoing study of adults above the age of 35 years. They included 1,317 people who had eaten any chocolate at all in the past year, and 824 who consumed dark chocolate regularly. Most people who ate dark chocolate consumed 5.7 grams per day. Individuals who ate dark chocolate had healthier diets overall than those who didn't; they were also younger and of higher social status, but less likely to exercise. The benefits were seen when people ate up to one 20-gram serving of dark chocolate every 3 days, but eating more chocolate wasn't more beneficial; in fact, effects on CRP levels "tended to disappear" at higher consumption levels, the researchers found.

A little exercise helps the severely obese
When it comes to exercise and physical activity, people who are severely obese often feel defeated and think — why bother. But a new study shows why they should bother. Even exercising an hour a week can boost their quality of life and ability to complete everyday tasks like getting dressed, tying shoes and simply moving around, the study found. The researchers examined the relationship between current activity levels and quality of life in 1,200 severely obese men and women entering a weight loss program. On average, these individuals were 100 pounds overweight. In a pre-program assessment, it was noted that patients who reported being physically active for just under 60 minutes a week, on average, had a better overall quality of life.

Bones may weaken after weight loss surgery
Patients lose bone density after weight loss surgery, and the more weight they lose, the greater the drop, new research shows. To investigate, they followed 23 men and women who had undergone Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery. This operation involves bypassing the duodenum, the portion of the small intestine that joins to the stomach—the chief site of calcium absorption by the body. Before the surgery, the patients had less-than-optimal blood levels of vitamin D, even though their intake of the nutrient was relatively high. After the surgery, they doubled their calcium intake and were consuming 2.6 times more vitamin D, but their blood levels of vitamin D remained low, and their blood levels of calcium actually fell. Signs of poor calcium absorption appeared within three months of the surgery. The density of their upper thigh bones had dropped by 9.2 per cent and their hip bone density fell by eight per cent but most patients didn't show loss of bone density in the lower back or the forearm.

Heading: Now, a metal macbook - Indian Express
Content:
A symbol of police brutality in 1991, Rodney King is appearing on TV to show he has overcome his addiction
On prominent display in Rodney King's suburban Rialto, California, home is a framed photograph—a reminder of his role in one of the most incendiary chapters in Los Angeles history. The close-up of a bulky, nervous King was taken during a 1992 news conference days after violence swept across the city following the acquittal of four Los Angeles Police Department officers who were charged with violating King's civil rights. King made his memorable plea for calm amid rioting that ultimately led to 54 deaths, more than 2,300 injuries and 12,000 arrests: "People, I just want to say—Can we all get along?"

In the more than 16 years since, King continues to ask himself that very same question. He is again putting himself—and his demons—front and centre in VH1's Celebrity Rehab with Dr. Drew, which launches its second season October 23. The series is billed as television's first examination of the rehabilitation process and features Drew Pinsky, the low-key celebrity physician who is well known for his radio call-in show, Loveline.

King said he appeared on the show to demonstrate that he has reformed. "Over the years, a lot of rappers—Lil' Wayne, Ice Cube—have used my name in their songs," said the 43-year-old King, who had his first drink when he was 8. "But they don't know me as a person. Putting myself out there is a good way for me to overcome the addiction."

"Waking up sober is a good day," said King as he relaxed in the home he shares with his fiancee, Dawn Jean, whom he has been with for six years. "I love being able to wake up and do positive things, to go to the gym." He also works with teenagers, coaching baseball for the city's recreation and parks department. He blames his alcoholism for much of his legal problems, which have included at least six arrests, including two for drunken driving and two for domestic abuse involving his former wife, his mother and one of his daughters. He has served more than 300 days in jail.

King voluteered to have his more negative side exposed for Celebrity Rehab. Last season's patients included Jeff Conaway (Taxi, Grease), Brigitte Nielsen (Rocky IV) and Daniel Baldwin (The Sopranos). The show also sparked controversy about the ethics of violating the privacy of rehab patients. The participants are filmed by hidden cameras throughout the facility and camera crews 24 hours a day as they go through a 21-day programme at a Pasadena residential treatment facility.

When King is first seen, he is a man on the edge. "I love alcohol, that's what I do," he says and pours a beer down his throat. It was an Alcoholics Anonymous sponsor who referred him to the show. King's first hours at the Pasadena centre were awkward. In the early episodes he is often separated from the group. Indeed, some of his fellow participants aren't sure who he is—one thinks he's an athlete, others believe he was in Boyz N the Hood.
